World.title: Drug trafficker, associates convicted after investigation Winnipeg police feared was undermined by corrupt cop
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A high-level cocaine trafficker, a nightclub owner working as a drug courier and a recently divorced father have pleaded guilty to various roles in a drug bust Winnipeg police once worried had been compromised by a corrupt officer.

Mohamed Ali, Abdullah Khan and Ahmed Dini were charged in 2024 as part of Project Roasted, a months-long investigation into a drug trafficking network. It culminated in one of the accused being arrested at his home and the other two being taken into custody as they left Stella's on Pembina Highway with about two kilograms of cocaine in one of their cars.

Months later, police got a warrant to search one of the men's seized cellphones because of "concerns that the drug investigation had been compromised" and a belief the phone data would establish a link between Ali, his associates and then-Winnipeg police officer Elston Bostock, an agreed statement of facts filed during Bostock's sentencing said.

"I believe that Ali and other members of the organized crime world in Winnipeg are receiving police information from … Bostock," a detective sergeant wrote in a warrant document filed to search Ali's phones.

Bostock, then a veteran constable, was sentenced this year to seven years in prison after admitting to a long list of corruption-related offences, including providing confidential police information to people outside the force.

When police went through the cellphone data, they found photos of Bostock with people the agreed facts described as "criminal associates" and text messages between Ali and others referencing Bostock looking up police information for them.

While few details about those targeted in Project Roasted were previously shared, recent court hearings shed light on the three men who have now been convicted in the case — and how some of them became involved in the drug operation.

Cocaine in Winnipeg, Niverville

A federal prosecutor told Court of King's Bench Justice Shawn Greenberg during a hearing in June that information about Ali's cocaine trafficking activities sparked Project Roasted.

The ensuing investigation included search warrants that allowed police to do repeated covert entries at Ali's home in Niverville, Man., south of Winnipeg. Investigators found cocaine, cutting agents, large amounts of cash and other drug-related items throughout the house and garage, in addition to the two kilograms later seized after Ali and Khan were arrested outside Stella's.

While Khan was moving the drugs around, Ali was the one directing those meetings, court heard.

"The accused was a high-level cocaine trafficker with some decision-making authority or responsibility," Deniset said.

Ali admitted to possessing cocaine for the purposes of trafficking in Winnipeg and Niverville from October 2023 to February 2024. Deniset said lawyers plan to jointly recommend he get eight years in prison at a sentencing expected to happen early next year.

Club owner's involvement 'baffling': judge

During Khan's sentencing in May, court heard the drug courier was the owner of the Moonlight Lounge nightclub on Osborne Street at the time of the investigation and had no criminal record.

His lawyer, Brett Gladstone, said he believed Khan's "poverty-related concerns," debts and other financial challenges contributed to the decisions his client made in the drug case and another incident he was later charged in.

Khan admitted to picking up a load of 20 kilograms of cocaine and delivering some of it before he was arrested with two kilos still in his car. He pleaded guilty to possession for the purpose of trafficking.

Khan also pleaded guilty to attempting to obstruct justice in a separate case, after he misled police following a shooting at his nightclub last year. He was sentenced to a total of seven years during an emotional hearing in May, where Khan apologized through tears for his actions.

"It's an individual who simply wants to do better," Gladstone said. "He regrets deeply the choices that he's made."

Provincial court Judge Kael McKenzie said it was "baffling" why Khan, who court heard is almost 50, was involved in the drug operation — but said it wasn't lost on him that the accused was running a nightclub at the time.

"I don't know if this is where you made these acquaintances," McKenzie said. "But it's probably not unusual, from where I sit, that people who are involved in nightclubs come across people who are involved in other things."

While a spokesperson for the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority of Manitoba previously said Moonlight Lounge's liquor licence was suspended in February 2025, the authority said this week it later got notice the business had been sold, with a request to withdraw its licence effective May 1, 2025.

'Regretted every day since'

In a sentencing in August 2025, court heard Ahmed Dini, described as a hard-working father in his 40s who'd spent years working with people with developmental disabilities, was also among those arrested in Project Roasted.

Court heard the same day police arrested Ali and Khan outside of Stella's, they did a search of Dini's apartment and found 213 rocks of crack cocaine stashed in a dresser drawer. His lawyer, Eric Wach, said Dini agreed to keep drugs there while at the "lowest point" of his life, as he dealt with a divorce and hard financial times.

"A friend of his said, 'Hey, there's an opportunity to make some money and, you know, stash some drugs and so forth,'" Wach said. "He took that opportunity, and it's something that he's regretted every day since. He talks about praying every day for forgiveness."

Provincial court Judge Lisa LaBossiere said she was "puzzled" why, despite Dini's financial circumstances, he'd involve himself "in something like this" as a father of eight children.

"The repercussions, even on your family alone, are significant," she said.

Dini was given a roughly two-year conditional sentence, to be followed by two years of supervised probation, as part of a joint recommendation from lawyers.

Charges against two other co-accused in Project Roasted were stayed last year. A spokesperson for federal prosecutors declined to provide specific reasons for the decisions to stay those charges.

World.title: 50% tariffs might mean U.S. businessowners have no choice but to leave their Canadian suppliers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Late last August, Julia Hallman and her husband road-tripped from their home in Massachusetts to spend time with one of their Canadian suppliers at Fromagerie La Station in Quebec.

Hallman sat on the back porch at the farmstead in Compton and watched the grazing cows that would eventually provide the milk for one of her shop's best-selling cheeses: the supple Alfred le Fermier. She's determined to keep buying the cheese to sell at her shop not only because her customers love it, but also because she counts the family as her friends.

"At the end of the day, we want to help support them and get more money into their hands," said Hallman, who owns Formaggio Kitchen, a specialty cheese and artisan goods shop in Cambridge.

Hallman is one of the innumerable businessowners in Canada and the U.S. waiting to hear whether the Trump administration will impose steep new levies on a long list of Canadian goods on Wednesday. Entrepreneurs south of the border say sustained, 50 per cent tariffs would force them to make the choice they've been trying to avoid for more than a year and a half: breaking away from longstanding, good-faith relationships with Canadian suppliers for the sake of their finances.

Hallman, left, at Fromagerie La Station in Compton, Que., last summer. (Submitted by Julia Hallman)

Businesses can only handle so much: owner

Imported products from cheeses to chocolates to spices and spreads account for roughly half of the stock at Formaggio Kitchen, with Canadian products making up roughly 15 per cent of those goods.

Hallman has managed tariffs on Canadian dairy in the past by sacrificing profit, raising prices for customers or both. She would like to continue that way, but says a rate of 50 per cent would eventually be too much to handle.

"There will come a point in time when we do have to make some hard choices," said Hallman, whose trip took her thousands of kilometres to several stops in Quebec.

"That's the challenge: We don't want to sacrifice the friendships that we've made. But we also have a threshold of what we can handle as a business and what our customers are willing to pay."

WATCH | Trade talks stuck at an impasse with days to go: Canada-U.S. trade talks stuck as Washington, provinces refuse to budge | Duration 5:14 Sources tell CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear looming new U.S. tariffs may be unavoidable as Washington continues to demand an end to provincial bans on U.S. alcohol — which provinces refuse to do. Canada's push for greater tariff relief on key sectors like lumber is also stalled.

Like Hallman, Sarah Paxton is worried the new rate will force her to move away from the suppliers her business has used in Ontario and Quebec for decades — one of which, Amisco, offered to meet her in the middle by covering the cost of tariffs until a certain date. She said she could manage the new fees herself for a while, but not forever.

"We're going to try and continue if we can. Fifty per cent, though, that's a pretty high number," said Paxton, who co-owns a contemporary furniture store in Richmond, Va., called LaDIFF.

"If you can imagine somebody reaching into your wallet and taking half of what you've got, that would be pretty tough."

The latest round of U.S. tariffs are set to hit $28-billion worth of Canadian goods just after midnight unless the two governments come to a last-minute deal.

Canadian entrepreneurs are worried about tariffs taking a massive bite out of their profits if American buyers like Hallman and Paxton — the ones who ultimately pay the bill when they bring Canadian goods across the border — have to source elsewhere.

Representatives from Canada and the U.S. met on Monday for what was expected to be the final meeting at the ministerial level. The Prime Minister's office confirmed to CBC News that Mark Carney spoke to U.S. President Donald Trump that afternoon about the "ongoing trade negotiations."

WATCH | Carney on the state of the negotiations as of Monday afternoon: Carney expects to speak with Trump before Aug. 19 tariff deadline | Duration 1:33 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he'll have 'opportunities over the next 48 hours' to speak to U.S. President Donald Trump before his threat to raise tariffs on a number of Canadian goods takes effect. Carney was speaking to reporters after announcing $10 billion in federal financing for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric agreement between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Waiting to see whether another threat would come to pass, Hallman stocked her shop's basement "cheese cave" with as many non-perishable goods as she could before the deadline. The cost of tariffs, she said, is just as emotional as it is financial.

"We're pretty stubborn," said Hallman. "We bring these products in intentionally. We bring them in because we love them. We don't want somebody to say, essentially, that we can't import them. That's what they're doing by putting a tariff that egregious [in place.]"

"It's a pretty loud and clear message."

World.title: Hoekstra's missteps in Canada are mild compared to some of Trump's ambassadors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. ambassador to Canada's behaviour has clearly rubbed many Canadians the wrong way.

Over 225,000 of them signed a House of Commons petition to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata — the rarely used diplomatic lever to kick an ambassador out of the country.

Jeremy Kinsman, who held important posts including ambassador to Moscow, London and the EU during his career as a Canadian diplomat, says Hoekstra's actions don't rise to the level that would normally lead to such a step.

"PNG is for egregious behaviour," such as malfeasance and direct interference in Canadian affairs, he said. But that doesn't mean Kinsman is an admirer of Hoekstra's.

WATCH | More about the petition: Why Canadians are targeting Trump’s U.S. ambassador | About That | Duration 2:24 More than 225,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling for the expulsion of Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada. Avneet Dhillon explains the reasons behind the petition, which comes as the latest trade deadline approaches. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

In diplomacy, said Kinsman, it's important to separate the messenger from the message. The problem of the Trump administration — embodied by Hoekstra — is that an already unpalatable message is being delivered by an undiplomatic messenger.

"[Hoekstra] does express frustration, exasperation, grievance with Canada that Canadians find bizarre.… Seemingly we're supposed to submit, quietly, docilely and accept all this stuff," Kinsman said.

"What the president of the United States thinks is offensive, it's hostile, it's aggressive, it's uninformed, it's untruthful. And [Hoekstra] radiates it."

The U.S. Embassy has declined to comment on the petition beyond acknowledging its existence.

No desire to explain

Some American career diplomats have observed the Trump era with dismay.

John Dinkelman ended a 37-year career last year, and was elected by his peers to head the American Foreign Service Association — essentially the diplomats' union.

Being a diplomat is not about being nice, said Dinkelman, but it is also not about gratuitously alienating your hosts.

"The idea behind diplomacy is to actually arrive at a point where your foreign interlocutor sees the logic your way and you are actually perceived to be doing — if not effectively doing — things for the betterment of all," he said.

"You've got to at least explain for your audience — the Canadian public — the context of it. He doesn't do that," Kinsman said.

Kinsman says Hoekstra's attitude has echoes of Chinese ambassador Lu Shaye, who picked several fights with his hosts during a low-water mark in Canada-China relations, including accusing the country of " white supremacy " over the arrest of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou.

Lu had already moderated his tone somewhat by the time he left Canada in 2019, and today, China seems to have decided the aggressive "wolf warrior" diplomacy he represented isn't that effective.

U.S. ambassadors, said Kinsman, are now the ones throwing their weight around and offending hosts.

"In Europe where their ambassadors are doing this sort of stuff, the United States is held in esteem today in percentage terms at about half of what Europeans now hold for China. What kind of a win is that?" he said.

Hoekstra has certainly fared no worse in Canada than he did as ambassador to the Netherlands during Trump's first term, when he found himself having to apologize after making false claims about Muslim "no-go zones" and politicians being set on fire .

And he's hardly unique among political ambassadors of the Trump era. Nor is Canada alone in having a petition to refuse credentials. Iceland had one after its new ambassador-designate, former Missouri congressman Billy Long, joked that he would turn the country into the 52nd state with himself as its governor.

He later apologized , something not all Trump ambassadors have elected to do.

Trump's ambassador to Chile, former U.S. Border Patrol agent Brandon Judd, made it his business to condemn Chileans who criticize Trump or his policies, including Chile's former left-wing president Gabriel Boric, and to attack ministers in the new right-wing government of José Antonio Kast who dared to criticize U.S. tariffs.

"He knows nothing about diplomacy," commented former Chilean foreign minister José Miguel Insulza this month.

When Ambassador Tom Rose began his tenure in Warsaw in late 2025, President Donald Tusk greeted him as "a true friend of Poland" who "understands our external and internal situation very well."

Two months later, Tusk was tweeting , "Mr. Ambassador Rose, allies should respect, not lecture, each other. At least that is how we, here in Poland, understand partnership."

That was after Rose announced that the U.S. would have "no further dealings, contacts, or communications" with the Speaker of Poland's legislature, for expressing the view that Trump didn't deserve the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ambassador barred from meeting French officials

Though it's perhaps the U.S. ambassador to France, Charles Kushner, who has most upset his hosts.

Kushner, a convicted fraudster and the father of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, wrote an open letter last summer accusing France of tolerating antisemitism and chiding it for moving toward the recognition of Palestine, saying "antizionism is antisemitism, pure and simple."

France responded that Kushner's "allegations are unacceptable" and "contravene international law" by interfering in domestic affairs. Kushner was summoned to the French diplomatic headquarters in Paris, the Quai D'Orsay, but failed to show.

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with U.S. Ambassador to France Charles Kushner in June. Kushner was twice summoned by the French government over the last year. (Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images)

He ignored a second summons two months later when the U.S. Embassy spoke out about "violent radical leftism" after the killing of French neo-fascist activist Quentin Deranque.

France has since banned Kushner from meeting any French official, citing his "misunderstanding of the basic expectations of an ambassador who has the honour of representing his country."

Next door in Belgium, the country's foreign minister responded angrily earlier this year to U.S. Ambassador Bill White's "personal attacks" around laws requiring medical certification for circumcision , saying his actions "violate basic diplomatic norms."

Then there's Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who is popular with his Israeli hosts, but who managed to offend every other government in the Middle East by saying that the Bible gives to the Jews all the land "from the Nile to the Euphrates, which is, once again, basically the entire Middle East," and adding "it would be fine if they took it all."

Key posts left unfilled

What troubles professional diplomats like Dinkelman is that when Trump doesn't appoint obnoxious ambassadors, he often appoints no ambassador at all.

About half of all U.S. ambassadors' posts are currently vacant — even though Dinkelman says there are experienced, ready and willing diplomats to take those roles.

"It's quite painful for someone like myself who spent 38 years in the diplomatic corps to see the diminished importance of having the people on the ground where you need them, when you need them," he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff has been involved in many of the administration's most high-stakes foreign negotiations. (Daniel Heuer/Reuters)

Only 13 of 54 countries in Africa now have a U.S. ambassador. Russia has no U.S. ambassador, and neither does Ukraine.

Key allies in the Middle East, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, also have no ambassador.

Instead, the U.S. has come to rely more and more on "special envoys," the most prominent of whom is a private citizen who once said he would have no role in the second Trump administration: Jared Kushner.

Kushner was unable to obtain a security clearance to work in the U.S. government until the White House interceded. Today he and New York real estate investor Steve Witkoff are the duo that conduct the most sensitive foreign affairs missions, including negotiations with Russia, Israel and Hamas, which would normally be the purview of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Witkoff has at times appeared to try to exclude Rubio from meetings, or speak to world leaders before Rubio can . Rubio's State Department has complained about Witkoff's use of insecure communications.

On Sunday, Kushner met with Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt, and on Monday again it was Kushner, not a U.S. diplomat or even government employee, who met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu .

While governments might normally wish to avoid employing envoys with close personal ties to their foreign interlocutors, no such concerns seem to have impeded Kushner's role as go-between with Netanyahu, a family friend who was a guest at the their home in New Jersey and once even slept in Jared's bed .

Reporting directly to Trump, Kushner and Witkoff allow the president to circumvent the normal channels of U.S. diplomacy and restrict the circle of knowledge of what is actually being discussed and agreed upon.

"One of the biggest complaints from some of the most respected professional diplomats from this nation is that the diplomats are not even in the room when decisions are being made or negotiations are taking place," said Dinkelman.

"That speaks volumes."

World.title: Ambassador Bridge 'aggressively' pursued trucking clients amid Gordie Howe delay: industry rep
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As uncertainty swelled in recent months around the long-awaited opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, representatives from the privately-owned Ambassador Bridge up the Detroit River were “aggressively” pursuing trucking companies in an apparent bid to retain their business, according to an industry representative.

Lak Shoan, director of policy for the Ontario Trucking Association, said his organization started hearing from a “handful of members” about the bridge’s efforts around springtime.

“It wasn't something that they came to us with or anything like that,” he said. “It would just come up in conversations sort of, you know, ‘Have you heard that the Ambassador Bridge has been, you know, reaching out to more companies?’ And that's when we started hearing from a few more folks that this was occurring.”

Lak Shoan is the director of policy for the Ontario Trucking Association. He said his organization started hearing from a “handful of members” about the bridge’s efforts around springtime. (Submitted by Lak Shoan)

CBC Windsor contacted several Canadian trucking companies with cross-border operations to ask if the Ambassador Bridge had approached them with toll rate offers. Those who answered said they couldn’t discuss private business agreements, while others simply did not respond.

But in a now-deleted post from late July, a U.S. trucking union official ordered his members not to use the new publicly-owned crossing because of a contract with the Ambassador Bridge in which they were saving $240,000 on tolls per month.

“If we wanted to begin using the Gordie Howe bridge, the Ambassador Bridge would first have to be notified that we intend to terminate the current contract,” wrote UAW Local 212 Chair JT Barrett, who represents FCA Transport (Stellantis) drivers.

Toll rates and revenue were a key part of the months-long political saga to open the $6.4 billion Gordie Howe bridge, which the Canadian government paid for in full. The deal to open the crossing contains a provision giving the U.S. government the ability to block the new bridge from lowering tolls “below the average of comparable regional crossings.”

The wealthy Moroun family of Michigan, which has owned the Ambassador Bridge since 1979, ramped up its political influence efforts in the months before U.S. President Donald Trump suddenly threatened to block the new crossing from opening.

Though the bridge eventually opened to traffic on July 27, it came after a June opening was scrapped at the request of the U.S. government, according to Prime Minister Mark Carney .

A poster attributed to UAW Local 212 Chair JT Barrett published in late July 2026, after the opening of the Gordie Howe bridge. (Screenshot/Facebook)

Trump has been accused of trying to block the new bridge’s opening to benefit the Morouns.

Representatives for the Ambassador Bridge did not respond to questions before publication time. But a notice on their website suggests there is a cheaper toll program available to some trucking companies.

“Commercial customers with over 150 expected monthly crossings are eligible for new A-Pass Subscription Accounts,” the page reads. “These feature fixed monthly rates, determined based on expected crossings.”

Shoan said the trucking association doesn’t know the exact details of what the bridge was offering companies, but he believes “it was around retention or trying to attract fleets to use the Ambassador Bridge.”

He said his group welcomes “healthy competition” between the bridges, which can lead to lower toll costs for trucking companies.

Barrett’s Facebook post provided some financial specifics about the deal he said FCA Transport has with the Ambassador Bridge.

“Under that contract, we pay a flat rate of $160,000 per month, regardless of how many crossings are made,” he said.

The first wave of vehicles cross the newly-opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich., on July 27, 2026. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

“Before this contract, we were paying north of $400,000 per month on a per-crossing basis,” he continued.

Barrett did not respond to a request for comment. Stellantis declined to confirm whether its FCA Transport drivers are under an exclusive toll contract with the Ambassador Bridge.

“The opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge strengthens the single most important border crossing in North America,” the global automaker said in a statement. “We are looking forward to using this additional crossing to support our just-in-time operations across our manufacturing operations in both countries, improving the flow of goods for an integrated industry that depends on seamless logistics. As a matter of company policy, Stellantis does not comment on proprietary information."

Shoan said the uncertainty around the Gordie Howe bridge’s opening would have made any deals offered by the Ambassador Bridge appealing to trucking firms.

“If you look at the current economic climate, which has been unsettled over the last several months, businesses are looking for certainty wherever you can find it,” he said. “If there's an opportunity to look for certainty from a cost perspective, [...] most business owners would definitely take that peace of mind.”

World.title: No referendum with Trump around, says PQ ahead of October election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a post to social media Tuesday, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he doesn’t want to risk the debate being “hijacked by the ups and downs of American politics.”

PQ says referendum on Quebec independence won't happen while Trump in power

The Parti Québécois will not hold a referendum as long as U.S. President Donald Trump remains in power, party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced Tuesday morning.

In a news release, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wants to avoid having the issue "hijacked by the ups and downs of American politics."

"An issue as crucial as the political future of Quebec requires conditions that allow for an informed and calm debate," the PQ leader said.

He said the next government will be faced with "more than enough challenges" without calling a referendum.

"So I decided to completely defuse the argument that this would be the worst time to think about our future because of Trump, by ruling out the possibility of holding a referendum by the end of his second term," St-Pierre Plamondon explained.

Trump's second term is set to end on Jan. 20, 2029.

St-Pierre Plamondon said that, if elected, he would still consult Quebecers on the issue of independence during his first mandate, but only after Trump leaves office.

The announcement comes just over a week ahead of the official launch of the Quebec provincial election campaign. Voters are scheduled to head to the polls on Oct. 5.

Across the country, Canadians are waiting to hear what comes of last-minute negotiations to avoid a fresh batch of American tariffs expected to take effect this week.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the discussions are "delicate" and "intense." He plans to speak to his American counterpart before the Wednesday deadline to broker a mutually agreeable deal.

PQ leader seeks to appeal to anglophones

The separatist leader has promised to hold a referendum in his first mandate, and while anglophone voters have largely supported Liberals in the past, St-Pierre Plamondon has been making an appeal to them in recent weeks.

In an open letter published in the National Post last week, St-Pierre Plamondon said he has heard from anglophones who "share the same realities and concerns" as francophones in the province.

As examples, he points to issues related to the cost of living and purchasing a home as well as struggles in the education and health-care systems to provide sufficient services.

“We are all in the same boat,” he wrote. “We live under the same institutions. We pay the same taxes. We deserve the same high-quality public services and individual financial well-being."

In a recent poll published by Angus Reid and surveying just over 900 people, only 15 per cent of respondents said they would "definitely vote to leave" if a referendum were held today.

An additional 11 per cent responded they would "lean toward voting to leave."

Regardless, the PQ is ahead in the polls.

According to political aggregator 338Canada, the Parti Québécois holds a lead in overall voting intentions, placing them ahead of the Quebec Liberal Party and the governing Coalition Avenir Québec.

World.title: U.S., Iran each dig in on Strait of Hormuz positions as their tenuous pact officially expires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the U.S. has no planned talks with Iran, and none were scheduled, as Iran's top negotiator said the Strait of Hormuz will remain shut until the U.S. meets the conditions of ‌an interim deal inked in June.

The June deal, known as the memorandum of understanding, called for a halt to all military operations and set a 60-day deadline for an agreement to permanently end the war and resolve the longstanding dispute over Iran's nuclear activities. That period lapsed on Monday.

The two sides offered differing versions of reality on Tuesday, with Trump asserting on Truth Social that the strait was "open and operating," with all Iranian mines in the body of water "removed or detonated." Commercial traffic in the Hormuz has slowed to a trickle compared to activity before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran to begin the war on Feb. 28.

In an earlier post, Trump posted an image of a manufactured map that showed the Strait of Hormuz as "New U.S. Territory." Last month, as hostilities picked up again, the U.S. reinstated a naval blockade it first implemented in April, restricting all maritime shipping to and from Iranian ports in mid-July.

Iran's parliamentary Speaker and negotiator in previous talks with the U.S., Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, reiterated Tuesday that Tehran plans to maintain its grip on shipping traffic until Washington meet Iran's conditions.

"Until the United States fulfils its commitments under the agreement, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen assets, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts and implementing the other conditions to which it committed, the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen," he said in comments published by state media.

Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, speaker of Iranian parliament, is shown in Tehran on July 3. Qalibaf laid out a list of demands on Tuesday were Iran to negotiate with the U.S., saying Tehran plans to maintain its grip on the Strait of Hormuz. (West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

Ship struck in the Hormuz

The June memorandum called for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened but gave Iran a vaguely defined role in facilitating traffic, leaving open the possibility it could charge fees after the 60-day deadline. Iran has seized on that clause to claim control over the waterway, through which about one-fifth of the global oil and liquefied natural gas supply flowed before the war.

Each side accused the other of violating the terms of the June pact within a few weeks, with Iran firing on vessels along a route near the coast of Oman, and the U.S. striking inside of Iran. Tehran responded to those attacks by firing drones at Arab countries hosting American forces, like Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain.

The U.S. cancelled waivers issued as part of the deal that had allowed Iran to sell its oil internationally and Trump restored a blockade of Iran's ports.

Trump has rejected Iran's demands, saying it's Tehran that should pay war reparations and claiming the U.S. controls the strait, while hoping to outlast Iran with economic pressure in the form of the blockade and longstanding sanctions.

WATCH | Trump threatens to bomb Oman: Trump threatens to bomb Oman as Iran peace talks deadline expires | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 2:58 U.S. President Donald Trump is threatening to bomb Oman if it 'gets in the way' as Iran and Oman work on a plan to reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The threat comes as a 60-day negotiating period for the U.S. and Iran to reach a peace deal expires with no agreement announced.

On Tuesday, a projectile hit a ship as it sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the British military's U.K. Maritime Trade Operations centre.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility but the attack highlights the danger of attempting to transit the strait as Iran throttles shipping traffic, even as it finalizes negotiations with Oman on a plan to manage the passage that's critical to global supplies of oil and natural gas.

With negotiations between the U.S. and Iran stalled, Iran has been holding separate talks with Oman on a plan to manage ships transiting the strait, and said Monday it was finalizing details for a joint statement.

Trump reacted angrily, using an expletive to warn that the U.S. would bomb Oman if it "gets in the way." It was the second time since the war began that the president has threatened the country, a longtime strategic partner of Washington.

"I think Oman is a critical negotiator with Iran, so it doesn't make a ton of sense. It looks like he's just trying to make more enemies and that's not a strategy," Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat and retired naval officer, told CNN.

Following a meeting between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Omani counterpart Badr al-Busaidi, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that the Iranian-Omani deal could pave the way for Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations for a "comprehensive and permanent deal that addresses all concerns and enhances regional security and stability."

Six commodity ships transited the strait on Monday, of which three were exiting the Gulf and three were entering, Kpler ship-tracking data showed, compared with the 10-day average of 11 ships. On average, 125 vessels were crossing per day in February before the war started.

At the chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, 19 commodity vessels transited on Monday, Kpler data showed, lower than a 10-day moving average of 26 and Sunday's 33 crossings. Those figures are slightly below the averages seen between January and June.

World.title: Alberta librarians feeling anxious about complying with new restrictions ahead of Jan. 1 deadline
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Less than five months remain before libraries across Alberta hit a deadline to comply with new restrictions on their collections.

But with a heavy workload and rising costs potentially required to comply with the restrictions, some librarians have lingering questions about how the regulations will be applied.

The restrictions are a result of Bill 28, and call for Alberta's public libraries to restrict access to materials — including books, graphic novels, magazines, films, TV series and video games — that contain a visual depiction of a sexual act. The new regulations prevent anyone 15 years old or younger from using or borrowing the newly restricted materials without a parent or guardian's permission.

Libraries have until Jan. 1 to identify what to restrict, where to store them and decide how to regulate their access.

Lesley Moody, manager for the Olds Municipal Library, said some of the bill's supporters don't seem to realize this work is more complicated than pulling a few titles off the shelf.

Her library has a collection of roughly 1,500 graphic novels alone to comb through. In some novels with hundreds of illustrated panels, staff will need to search for what could be a handful of drawings that require a book to be restricted.

"Because there is no specific list being provided to us by the provincial government, it will require all of us to meticulously go through every single book in our graphic novel collections," Moody said.

Moody estimated her staff will need around 600 hours, translating to $15,000 in labour, just to review the graphic novels in their collection.

WATCH | Some librarians push back on new restrictions in Alberta: Alberta libraries raise concerns over 'censorship' in proposed new bill | Duration 2:31 The Coalition of Alberta Public Libraries is pushing back on Bill 28, saying there are serious concerns over privacy, local control and the future of library services.

The cost her library faces only gets higher to assess DVDs, video games and other books with images in their collection, buy new shelving units for the restricted materials, and create new workflows and policies around library cards for kids and parental permissions.

Moody said she's confident her staff is large enough to review their collection without needing to temporarily close to the public, but smaller libraries may have to take that step.

“If you only have one or two [staff] in a library and you have a deadline of January 1, possibly the only option for you is to completely close the library while you comply, which is a very sad thought for a lot of communities that need to have a public library open," said Moody.

Libraries waiting on new guidelines

The province has said it plans to release guidelines this month advising libraries how to adjust or create new policies in response to Bill 28, which Ron Sheppard, director of the Parkland Regional Library System, said he’s very anxious to see.

Sheppard said he wants to know if the restrictions will apply to educational materials, or to history books with pictures of Greek vases or ancient temples that feature explicit imagery.

He also wants to know whether libraries can rely on ratings systems for films and video games, rather than librarians needing to view entire collections.

LISTEN | Effect new restrictions could bring on Alberta libraries: Radio Active 9:40 Concerns are rising about how Bill 28 will impact Alberta libraries Banned books are a controversial topic in Alberta these days. This spring, the provincial government introduced legislation to ensure children and young teens won't be able to access sexually graphic images at public libraries. The government has emphasized they are not banning books, but merely creating safeguards for children and families. But what happens at public libraries when the books they offer are limited in this way? Toni Samek is a professor emeritus at the University of Alberta.

"There is a legal definition for pornography, and nothing, to my understanding, in any Alberta library meets that legal definition of pornography," said Sheppard, who is also a member of the Coalition of Alberta Public Libraries' steering committee.

"So then it becomes subjective."

Sheppard said some libraries with little free space have considered storing all restricted materials in a warehouse off-site or at regional library headquarters like Parkland's.

He also has questions about access to online resources. Boards are expected to apply the same restrictions to e-books and audiobooks, but Sheppard noted they are often borrowed through third-party vendors, like Libby, that are housed in another country.

Restricting access

Jack Alarie, press secretary for Alberta's Municipal Affairs ministry, said Bill 28 is only meant to ensure children do not stumble across explicit images in a public library.

“We’re talking about access controls, not censorship, and no library will be told to remove anything from its shelves,” said Alarie via email.

Libraries have already used professional standards for decades to curate their collections and separate materials based on what's age-appropriate, said Ken Feser, chief librarian at the Medicine Hat Public Library, and set up processes to take public complaints.

WATCH | New rules introduced for Alberta's public libraries: Why the Alberta government is telling libraries to put some books out of sight | Duration 2:05 Alberta’s municipal affairs minister says new rules will require public libraries to move any material with graphic sexual content so it can't be accessed by children or young teens.

Feser said he's concerned the new restrictions will make some materials less visible to the public, making them essentially disappear.

“Burying a book is almost as effective as burning a book, and they’re really asking us to bury these books,” said Feser.

“They need to be moved from public shelves, they need to be placed somewhere in some back corner or locked storage area where they can’t be viewed.”

He added he's concerned some libraries may eventually refuse to carry some books if they lead to too many complaints, or that a stigma could be attached to borrowing restricted books, similar to movies behind beaded curtains in old video stores.

Feser said the new restrictions treat libraries as adversaries, after years of co-operative work with the province.

“It’s an abrupt change and it has nothing to do with anything the libraries did," Feser said.

Staff at the Calgary Public Library's Memorial Park branch are required by the Libraries Act to ensure people below the age of 16 cannot access library materials with sexually explicit images, beginning Jan. 1. (Zazak Bouarab/Radio-Canada)

Calgary Public Library CEO Sarah Meilleur said she cannot speculate on how the new restrictions could affect their work, but that her team intends to update the public when they know more.

The province's decision follows a similar order to school libraries . Action4Canada was an interest group that celebrated the decision, and its founder, Tanya Gaw, expressed support last week for Bill 28’s new restrictions.

“Action4Canada believes it is of the highest priority to protect children's innocence. They should not be exposed to pornographic and sexually explicit materials within schools, school libraries or publicly-funded libraries. Period," said Gaw via email.

Expanded inspections

Bill 28 also gives an expanded scope for inspectors to investigate any matter related to a library’s management, administration or operation. But Sheppard said it's still unclear how the inspection process will work.

"It is an area of considerable angst for many library managers, because they don't know what will trigger an inspection," said Sheppard.

"They don't know if they will even know that there is a complaint lodged until an inspector shows up. They also don't know what kind of action they're going to be forced to take.”

Alarie said the inspections are no different from what already applies to municipalities, adding that the province expects them to occur rarely, with the intent to "fix problems, not to punish."

Kelsey Chic, library manager for the Carmangay and District Municipal Library, argued the inspection process risks taking too much authority away from local decision-making, after staff have typically curated collections tailored to their individual communities.

“It’s local people at a local level making decisions for the local people. I don’t need someone in Edmonton telling me what people in Carmangay need,” said Chic.

Carmangay is a village of just under 300 people, roughly 122 kilometres southeast of Calgary.

Throughout the summer, Chic has posted videos to social media informing her community about her criticisms of Bill 28, and how the library's operations could change. She said she wanted library users to know the issue wasn't as black and white as some may believe.

“They're like, 'Well yeah, we don't want kids reading porn.' No one does," Chic said. "We don't have porn in libraries, I promise you. Hustler is not next to our HGTV magazine."

James Turk, director at the Centre for Free Expression at Toronto Metropolitan University, said that according to his organization’s data, there have been just 85 challenges to books for children and young adults in Alberta libraries in the last decade, showing little basis to introduce new restrictions.

Libraries should bring a constitutional challenge forward against the restrictions, Turk said, arguing it limits freedom of expression rights for young library users.

Whether Alberta's libraries push back or not, Turk said librarians across Canada are watching closely to see how the restrictions in Alberta unfold.

"If this is successful in Alberta, libraries in the rest of the country are quite fearful there's going to be a major push, as there was in Alberta, to get legislation of this sort,” said Turk.

World.title: Evacuation order lifted for most of Summerland, B.C., more than 1 week after fire forced residents to flee
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After more than a week of stress and anxiety, most residents of Summerland, B.C., can return to their homes.

“It’s the news we’ve all been waiting for for the last week," Mayor Doug Holmes told CBC's Daybreak South.

The community of more than 12,000 was forced to flee after the Bald Range wildfire broke out on Aug. 7 and grew explosively, claiming the life of an 80-year-old woman.

Holmes said an evacuation order was lifted for 3,380 properties at 7 a.m. PT Tuesday, what he called "the majority of Summerland."

WATCH | First wave of Summerland evacuation orders lifted: Some Summerland wildfire evacuees get green light to come home | Duration 2:08

Orders for a smaller number of properties were lifted over the weekend.

As of Tuesday, 530 properties remain under an evacuation order in the Garnet Valley, Prairie Valley and Meadow Valley.

All other Summerland residents remain under evacuation alert and must still be ready to leave at a moment's notice.

A map showing parts of the Summerland area that remain under evacuation orders and alerts as of Aug. 18. (District of Summerland)

Holmes said those areas remain unsafe until geotechnical experts can test slope stability above the communities, and that Garnet Valley remains without power.

"I know there was a lot of frustration, people waiting, I was feeling frustrated myself," he said.

"But we had to do it properly, and orderly, and this is the big day.”

WATCH | Using art to process the trauma of wildfire evacuation: How art is helping Summerland evacuees process trauma | Duration 2:44



A boil water advisory remains in place due to the community's water treatment plant going offline during the evacuation.

The community's landfill is also still on fire, meaning trash will need to be trucked to a facility operated by the regional district.

On Monday, the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen said an initial assessment found the fire had damaged or destroyed about 150 structures.

About 40 of those structures were within the municipality's boundaries.

Holmes said people who had lost property were contacted by social workers and counsellors, and given the chance to see their homes before the order was lifted.

"We just thought it was really important that people were able to go and see their properties, that had lost their homes, before we opened it up to all of their neighbours," he said.

As of Tuesday, the 214-square-kilometre fire remained classified as out of control.

Firefighters have successfully held the fire behind control lines on the southern and eastern flanks, and have turned their attention to the fire's west side where it continues to show aggressive behaviour.

World.title: Weekend decorator: Adding pizzazz to an awkward room
World.content:
Article content

I hesitate to make my last suggestion because for the most part the room is working quite well, but if you’re feeling bold, you could get rid of all the furniture and try doing a symmetrical arrangement instead. Two small loveseats facing each other could work really well here and create a calmer atmosphere. There are a lot of lines, and a lot going on visually, and symmetry is often the answer to that problem. I’m imagining two caramel velvet sofas, small in scale, with two identical long and narrow coffee tables in front of each sofa. If there’s room, reuse your armchairs kitty corner to each sofa, facing the fireplace. You don’t need the lighting to be symmetrical and you could have the arc lamp on one site, a small table on the right side with a table lamp, and I would keep the idea of a sofa table behind the sofa separating the living and dining rooms. Everything should sit firmly on a larger rug, that could definitely have a smaller rug layered in the middle if you want to add some colour and texture. This is a dramatic idea but something to think about as a possible future move. If I had to prioritize this list, I would start with editing the knickknacks, removing the branches, buying a tree and adding a few pillows. That alone would add the punch I think you are craving.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.
