A team is currently in Belize at present checking projects funded by the agency and talking to beneficiaries.

World.title: The back-to-school lines at Melchor are a referendum, and Belize keeps losing it
World.content:
The back-to-school lines at Melchor are a referendum, and Belize keeps losing it

By Horace Palacio:

Look closely at one number from last weekend, because it tells a whole national story.

On Saturday, our western border recorded 147 excursion passengers, the day-trippers who cross and return. On Sunday, that number exploded to 1,613. Eleven times higher in twenty four hours. That is not tourism. That is not family visits. That, my friends, is the great Belizean back-to-school shopping run, in a single statistic.

Ministry of Immigration data shows 4,903 passenger movements through the Western Border over August 15 and 16, up from 4,725 for the same weekend last year, a 3.8 percent increase. Behind those numbers stand Belizean mothers and fathers, lists in hand, crossing into Melchor de Mencos, Guatemala, for uniforms, undershirts, socks, shoes, and school supplies, ahead of the new academic year.

Now, before a single word more, let me say what must be said first.

Do not shame those families. Do not dare. That mother in the line is not disloyal to Belize. She is loyal to her children, exactly as she should be. She has done the arithmetic this column has begged Belizeans to do, counted her dollars twice, and gone where they stretch furthest. Her duty is to the three children she must dress by September, not to any merchant’s margin. If crossing a border saves her enough to buy the third pair of shoes, she is not the problem in this story.

She is the referendum. And Belize keeps losing it.

Run some honest, illustrative arithmetic. Suppose even half of those weekend crossings were shoppers, and suppose each spent a modest two hundred Belize dollars. That is roughly half a million dollars, in one weekend, at one border, before school even starts. Now add every other August weekend. Add the northern families making the same run to Chetumal. The true annual figure, nobody has counted. But every one of those dollars pays a Guatemalan shopkeeper’s rent, a Guatemalan worker’s wage, a Guatemalan government’s taxes, while the shops of San Ignacio, Benque, and Belize City watch their own customers drive past.

So the only question worth asking is the one nobody in authority seems to ask. Why is it cheaper to school-shop in another country?

The Guatemalan merchant is not a magician. He simply operates in a bigger market, closer to a real garment industry, Guatemala actually manufactures clothing, with cheaper wholesale channels and a lighter cost structure. Meanwhile, look at what a child’s uniform must survive to reach a Belizean shelf. An expensive port. Freight and fees. Import duty at the wharf. GST at 12.5 percent stacked on top of the duty-inflated price. And then the margins of a small, concentrated import trade this column has written about before, where thin competition lets prices rest fat. By the time that shirt hangs in a Belizean store, it wears more taxes and costs than the child will wear clothes. The mother is not fleeing Belizean merchants. She is fleeing the Belizean cost stack. Melchor did not win her. We drove her there.

Now, the wrong answer, and let us kill it before some official proposes it. The wrong answer is walls. Raise the exit fees, tighten the border, squeeze the shoppers back home. Understand what that does. It punishes the poorest families for the failure of the system, taxing the mother a second time for the crime of surviving the first tax. You do not keep customers by locking the shop door. You keep them by fixing the shop.

So here is how government fixes the shop. Seven policies, most executable before next August.

One. Zero-rate the school basket, permanently. Take GST off children’s uniforms, school shoes, exercise books, bags, and basic supplies. I made this exact recommendation in the minimum wage series, lighten the basket the poor actually buy. There is no basket more deserving than the one that dresses a child for school.

Two. Declare an annual back-to-school duty holiday. A two-week window each August when import duties on school essentials are suspended. Tax holidays for school shopping are a tested tool used across American states for decades. Give Belizean merchants two weeks each year to compete on level ground, and watch the lines move from Melchor to Albert Street.

Three. Sew the uniforms in Belize. A school uniform is one of the simplest garments made, and this country is full of skilled seamstresses and village sewing groups. Launch a national uniform initiative, duty-free fabric supplied to Belizean sewing cooperatives, and government-assisted schools directed to source Belizean-made uniforms, counting toward the twenty percent small-business procurement rule already promised under the new procurement law. Every uniform sewn here is a wage paid here.

Four. Bulk-buy like a nation. Belize already runs a textbook program that buys at scale. Extend the model. Let schools, PTAs, and credit unions pool orders for supplies at true wholesale prices, sold to parents at cost. The Guatemalan advantage is partly wholesale muscle. Four hundred thousand people buying separately have none. Organized, we have plenty.

Five. Attack the landed cost itself. Everything this column has said about the expensive port, slow customs, and the duty schedule lands directly on this school shirt. Review the duties on children’s essentials specifically. A country that taxes school clothes heavily should not act shocked when school shopping emigrates.

Six. Referee the margins. Where competition is thin, publish the numbers. Landed cost versus shelf price on staple school items, in the open, every August. Sunlight on margins does what a hundred press releases cannot. And it protects the honest merchant too, by proving who is fair.

Seven. Help the poorest through Belizean tills. Expand existing school assistance into a school-starter support for the neediest families, delivered as vouchers redeemable at Belizean merchants. The family gets the help. The dollar stays home. One policy, two victories.

And a word to our merchants, because government is only half of this. The border is your competition report card, delivered every August. Sharpen your sourcing. Pool your wholesale orders. Run your own back-to-school pricing like you mean to win the mother back. I wrote weeks ago that in this new economy, money moves from the waiting to the working. That applies on Albert Street too.

Here is the measure of success, plain and countable. Next August, the Ministry of Immigration will hand us this same weekend data. If the policies above are done, the excursion number shrinks, and the lines grow where they belong, outside Belizean shops, manned by Belizean workers, ringing Belizean tills.

The mothers are not waiting for speeches. They vote with their feet every August, in the most honest election this country holds.

Stop blaming the voters, Belize.

Win the vote.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Saldivar says youth in politics is nothing new, integrity is the real test
World.content:
Saldivar says youth in politics is nothing new, integrity is the real test

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Former Belmopan area representative John Saldivar has weighed in on the generational conversation stirring Belizean politics, arguing in a social media post that young leadership is neither new nor novel, and that the real test of any politician, young or old, is integrity under scrutiny.

Saldivar grounded the argument in history, including a chapter of his own rarely told. Recruited in 1992 at age 25 by then UDP Chairman Dean Lindo to become the party’s Cayo South candidate, he left on study leave to Mankato State University in May 1993, only for Prime Minister George Price to call snap elections weeks later. Party Leader Manuel Esquivel then struck a deal with NABR Leader Philip Goldson that handed Cayo South to an NABR candidate for the UDP/NABR coalition. “I therefore did not get my chance to be the candidate until 1998. I was still young at thirty one,” he wrote.

The precedents run deeper, he noted: Derek Aikman defeating a sitting Prime Minister in Freetown at 25 in 1984, Salvador Fernandez emerging as a Cayo star at 24 the same election, and Patrick Faber entering the House at 22 in 2003. “Injecting youth and energy into political parties is a part of the natural process of political evolution,” Saldivar wrote. “It’s not new politics versus old politics. It is good politics versus bad politics.”

His closing carried both blessing and warning. Wishing newcomers luck, he cautioned that some politicians “start out good, they even start out young, and then turn out to be bad,” and that success “will not be because of your age but because of the integrity, honesty, and vision you bring to the table and how you stand up to scrutiny once given the power.”

World.title: Belize takes crown at first Miss Black International Pageant hosted in country
World.content:
Belize takes crown at first Miss Black International Pageant hosted in country

By Zoila Palma: Belize made history on Saturday night as the country hosted the Miss Black International Ambassador pageant for the first time, welcoming contestants from several countries, including Ghana and Barbados.

Belize also celebrated major success at the event, with Maryam Abdul-Qawiyy crowned Ms. Black International Ambassador and D’Ancy Ramclam taking the title of Teen Black International Ambassador.

Former Miss Universe Belize titleholder Ashley Lightburn served as the National Director for Belize and said the team had only about seven weeks to select and prepare the delegates. “We had roughly, I think, seven weeks to select and train our delegates,” Lightburn explained.

Belize ultimately fielded representatives in three categories, with Maryam Abdul-Qawiyy, D’Ancy Ramclam and Felicia Alas selected to represent the country.

Lightburn said the results demonstrated the strength of Belize’s representatives, particularly Abdul-Qawiyy, who stood out across several areas of the competition.

“Maryam won, I think, there were like eight different categories of additional prizes that she could have won and she took at least six of those,” Lightburn said.

Abdul-Qawiyy captured awards including Best Costume, Best in Interview and Best in Evening Gown, in addition to winning the Ms. Black International Ambassador crown.

The National Director also commended both delegates for taking part despite the short preparation period and challenges associated with pageant participation.

World.title: STEM U Foundation opens evening welding classes for working adults
World.content:
STEM U Foundation opens evening welding classes for working adults

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): One of the country’s best-paying trades just became easier to enter without quitting your day job. STEM U Foundation has opened registration for its Adult Evening Welding Classes, a 16 week program starting August 31 at the STEM U Welding Lab at St. Ignatius High School.

The training is hands-on in MIG (GMAW) and Stick (SMAW) welding, with a certification opportunity in two positions, credentials aligned with American Welding Society standards that travel on any resume, local or abroad.

The program is built around working schedules. Students choose between weekday evenings, Monday, Tuesday and Friday from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m., or a single Saturday session from 1:00 to 6:00 p.m., six hours weekly either way.

Tuition is BZ$1,150 with a payment plan available, and enrollment is capped at 18 seats, so spaces are genuinely limited.

Skilled welders remain in demand across construction, agriculture, marine and fabrication work countrywide, and a certified torch hand rarely sits idle.

Applications are through the link on STEM U Foundation’s pages (https://forms.cloud.microsoft/r/bJmt34Btvr), with inquiries to [email protected]. Your future starts here, and it starts August 31.

World.title: Belize dries out as sunshine returns
World.content:
Belize dries out as sunshine returns

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize turns the corner toward drier weather today, with conditions becoming relatively dry later in the day, sunshine breaking through, and only a few morning showers over central and northern areas standing between the country and a fair midweek.

According to the National Meteorological Service, skies will be sunny with cloudy spells today and cloudy at times tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with a few more likely over central and northern areas this morning, then over the south tonight.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 88 degrees Fahrenheit (31 Celsius) and a low of 83 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will climb to 93 degrees Fahrenheit (34 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius).

At sea, conditions run choppy, with easterly winds of 10 to 15 knots and waves of 3 to 5 feet, workable water with the usual care for smaller craft.

On the tropical front, the calm holds. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead to Wednesday and Wednesday night, mainly fair and warm conditions take over, with only isolated showers or isolated thunderstorms developing.

Today’s low tides are at 8:30 AM and 7:50 PM, with a high tide at 2:10 PM and another high at 1:52 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:36 AM and will set at 6:16 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Derrick Rudon.

World.title: Ministry of Sustainable Development provides update on fish kill, anti-littering and environmental protection
World.content:
Ministry of Sustainable Development provides update on fish kill, anti-littering and environmental protection

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change held a press conference on August 17, 2026, to highlight key environmental issues and ongoing initiatives aimed at protecting Belize’s natural resources.

Representatives from the Belize Forest Department, Climate Change Department, and Department of the Environment (DOE) provided updates on their respective areas of work.

The DOE also addressed the ongoing fish kill issue, emphasizing the need for continued monitoring and public awareness as authorities work to better understand and respond to environmental concerns.

The Department further reinforced the importance of Belize’s National Anti-Littering Campaign, reminding the public that keeping the country clean and protecting its natural environment is a shared responsibility. Officials encouraged greater public participation and collective action to address environmental challenges.

The Ministry stressed that environmental protection is everyone’s business and called on citizens to play their part in protecting Belize for future generations.

World.title: Police detain pickup driver following fatal crash in Billy White, Cayo
World.content:
Police detain pickup driver following fatal crash in Billy White, Cayo

By Zoila Palma: Police have detained a 26-year-old man as part of an ongoing investigation into a fatal road traffic accident that claimed the life of 37-year-old Marcello Moh of Santa Familia Village and left 18-year-old Aidan Humes injured.

The collision occurred at around 2:32 a.m. on Sunday, August 16, 2026, in Billy White Village, Cayo District.

According to Police ASP Stacy Smith, Staff Officer, “Police have detained a 26 year old male person as a part of an ongoing investigation into a road traffic accident” involving a pickup truck, a motorcycle and a bicycle. Smith said initial investigations indicate that the detained man was travelling in an F-150 pickup truck from Billy White Village toward Santa Familia Village when, upon reaching a curve, “collision occurred between that vehicle he was traveling in and the motorcycle which was being driven by Humes as well as a bicycle that was being by Moh.”

Both Moh and Humes sustained injuries in the collision, but Moh later succumbed while receiving treatment.

Humes, who suffered serious injuries, was transported for medical care.

Smith confirmed that “Both Moh and Humes sustained injuries in the course of the collision,” adding that Moh “who received grave injuries succumbed while undergoing treatment.”

Police and Scenes of Crime personnel responded to the area and commenced investigations into the circumstances surrounding the crash.

Police reportedly detained the driver of the pickup pending investigation.

ASP Smith added that “The circumstance of the collision remains under investigation.”

World.title: Hospital death probe
World.content:
An undated photo of Kenise Dunn, who died at the St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days after giving birth.

ADMINISTRATORS at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital say they have launched a probe into the death of Kenise Dunn, who died at the facility five days after giving birth.

With family demanding answers into the circumstances surrounding Dunn’s death, the hospital’s Chief Executive Officer Dennis Morgan told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that with internal investigations ongoing the hospital is not able to provide a statement on the matter.

According to Morgan, the investigation is integral in allowing all the facts to be found and confirmed, and for the family to be given factual answers.

Morgan added that the hospital could not legally disclose information about any patient to anyone who is not listed as their next of kin, and the administrators are already in contact with the relevant family member who has been cooperative with staff as the investigation continues.

Acknowledging the concerns held by the wider family, Morgan advised other relatives of Dunn to reach out with their questions either by calling or visiting the hospital, where they will be welcomed and briefed as best as possible.

But for Kirk Hall, uncle of the deceased, information surrounding the death of Dunn is long overdue.

Hall charged that since Dunn, who he affectionately called Punky, was admitted to hospital on July 29 up until her death on Friday, August 14, the medical staff interacting with her have not been willing to provide any information.

Tearfully recounting his niece’s last days, Hall on Monday told the Observer that Dunn, who was eight months’ pregnant, complained to him on July 27 about intense stomach pains and not being able to pass her stool for at least three days.

When told of her complications, Hall referred her to the hospital for checks to rule out anything beyond simple constipation and to ensure she received the necessary treatment.

He said when checking on his niece during her stay at the hospital he was still unable to get any information from the medical personnel as to what was causing her pain.

“When she went down there she called me and said, ‘Uncle Kirk, they might have to admit me.’ Days gone by and I asked what was going on, and she said, ‘The doctors, they keep just coming and pulling blood.’ Every day they just kept pulling blood from her while her belly continued to hurt,” said Hall.

“I said, ‘Punky I know how you feel, but it soon over.’ She called me last week, Friday [August 7] morning. So all this time, from the 29th, she has been there up ‘til when she called me…nothing had been done to her,” claimed Hall.

According to Hall, the numerous blood tests she had informed him of never provided any results, and his only update was that Dunn needed to do an ultrasound at a nearby medical facility, but no ambulance was available and the hospital was short-staffed.

“She said to me, ‘Uncle Kirk, they are supposed to carry me to go do an ultrasound. I hear the nurse just come and tell me they’re short of staff so they are not going to carry me, and the ambulance is not going to work.’ So I said, ‘Punky, what do you mean by they are short of staff and don’t have an ambulance?’ I said, ‘I’m coming to you either tomorrow or Sunday,’ ” Hall added.

He told the Observer that his Sunday visit was only more worrisome as Dunn, 33, could not tell him what was wrong with her and doctors refused to speak with him.

“When I saw her, she was on the stretcher and everything, but I can tell you, she was in pain. I said, ‘Punky, what happened?’ She said, ‘Uncle Kirk, I feel pain, man. Pain, pain, pain.’ So I said, ‘What did the doctor say?’ She said, ‘I can’t talk to them no more. You go ask them, ask them what happened to me.’

“So I went to the nurse and I asked her, ‘What’s going on with her? Can I speak to the doctor behind you?’ The nurse told me to have a seat, and about 10, 15 minutes later she came back and said the doctor says my niece can talk [for herself] and I’m not the next of kin, so she can’t talk to me,’ ” relayed Hall.

Following his visit he received a call from Dunn the next day that she was being taken to have the ultrasound done. By Tuesday it was revealed to him, by a relative who he says works at the hospital, that she had given birth.

Shortly after, he said he was told by that relative that a doctor advised him that she needed emergency surgery.

According to Hall, on that day, August 9, Dunn was placed on life support.

He said doctors briefed the family that she was gravely ill, after surgery revealed a tumour believed to be cancerous that was found in her colon. Hall charged that compounding her afflictions, the doctors said they removed the colon, and two litres of stool from her body after a bowel rupture.

Dunn never recovered, passing away five days later.

Now, the family is overcome by grief and riddled with questions. Why was the family not told about the results from the blood tests or the ultrasound? Why was she allowed to give birth naturally after being admitted for constipation? Was it ever confirmed that the tumour was malignant; was there a biopsy done? Was there even, ever a tumour?

Hall’s frustration was palpable, his voice breaking as he became overcome by emotion.

“We have requested all of that. We were told on Saturday that an investigation is going to be launched. This morning [Monday], persons from the Ministry of Health reportedly went in and seized all form of records when it come to her and the doctors, whatever they said and did to her and all of that. She didn’t deserve to die like that, man. Had there been proper care and compassion she wouldn’t die, man,” charged Hall

“We are waiting with bated breath to see what the findings are, what the results are,” Hall added.

World.title: Robinson sounds alarm on Jamaica’s economy
World.content:
ROBINSON... we will continue to agitate, we will continue to recommend and we will continue to hold the Government accountable so that Jamaica can have a better economy.

Opposition spokesman on Finance Julian Robinson says Jamaicans are facing a worsening cost-of-living crisis while the economy struggles to grow, blaming the Andrew Holness-led Administration for failing to take decisive action to ease the pressure on households.

Robinson, who was speaking at the annual constituency conference of fellow People’s National Party (PNP) parliamentarian Phillip Paulwell, at Vauxhall High School in Kingston Eastern and Port Royal on Sunday, said the economic challenges facing Jamaicans are being compounded by rising energy costs and the slow pace of recovery following Hurricane Melissa.

Robinson acknowledged that Hurricane Melissa, which struck Jamaica on October 28, 2025, would inevitably have affected economic activity, but argued that the Government’s response to the disaster had worsened the economic fallout.

“We have had two consecutive quarters of negative growth which means we are in a recession. We are likely to have a third quarter of negative growth and the main reason why the economy continues to flounder, we knew we had Hurricane Melissa which would have triggered at least one quarter, but the very slow pace of recovery by the Government is what is contributing to the negative growth. It is taking too long, particularly for those who are in the affected parishes in the west, to get the assistance so that they can get back on their feet,” argued Robinson.

He pointed to the latest Ministry of Finance report, which he said showed a $28.6-billion shortfall in tax revenues, and charged that the gap would place additional pressure on Government finances and force it to either reduce expenditure or dip into the capital budget. He also blamed the shortfall partly on the slow pace of assistance to hurricane-affected businesses.

But Robinson’s criticism extended beyond the impact of Melissa.

He linked the country’s economic difficulties to the cost of energy and the vulnerability of consumers to movements in global oil prices.

According to Robinson, Jamaica could do more to cushion households and businesses against higher oil prices by expanding its use of renewable energy.

“They have not added one megawatt of renewable energy to the grid. What has been done in the last 10 years is what we started when we were last in office. So while you can’t control the price of oil, you can control how much renewable energy is added to the grid and they have failed miserably at adding whether it is solar, whether it is wind,” he pointed out.

Robinson also criticised the Government’s decision to abolish the oil-price hedge, arguing that consumers have not been given another mechanism to shield them from sharp increases in fuel prices.

Beyond the immediate pressure on household budgets, Robinson said the economy was also struggling with a mismatch between the skills employers require and the workers available to fill those positions.

“We have not heard any policy or programme to deal strategically with what employers are bawling about when they say they can’t find people to work, even though every one of us as representatives can point to hundreds, maybe thousands of people who are looking for work. So there’s a clear mismatch between what employers want and what is in the market,” he said.

Robinson proposed that the Government provide financial grants to employers to train and up-skill their workers, arguing that businesses themselves are best positioned to identify the specific skills and training needed to address the gap between the skills employers require and those available in the labour market.

He ended his remarks by insisting that the Opposition would continue to press the Government on its economic policies while offering alternatives that, “could improve growth and living conditions”.

“We will continue to agitate, we will continue to recommend and we will continue to hold the Government accountable so that Jamaica can have a better economy that will suit not just a few people but all of Jamaica,” declared Robinson.

World.title: Triple L, Rytikal encourage with Keep On Fighting
World.content:
Rytikal.

For producer Triple L, music has always been about more than creating infectious rhythms. With his latest production, Keep On Fighting, featuring dancehall artiste Rytikal, he is using sound to speak directly to people navigating the pressures of everyday life.

The track, set for release on August 21 via Triple L Records, is rooted in the realities Triple L says he sees around him, from financial pressures, other stresses, and disappointment.

“[It was inspired by] real life. I see too many people around me getting knocked down but still getting back up. Dealing with bills, stress, and doors closing in their faces. I wasn’t trying to complain about it. I wanted to create something that tells people that the pressure isn’t here to break you; it’s here to build you. Keep on fighting,” he said.

For Triple L, Rytikal was an obvious choice to deliver the message because of his ability to connect with songs rooted in struggle.

“Because he has lived it. He doesn’t just sing about struggle; he feels it. When he gets on a track like this, you believe him. He has the pain and the fire. He is one of the voices for people who are tired but still standing,” he said.

The collaboration came together organically.

“I built the track specifically for him [Rytikal] and reached out to my cousin, who has a better connection with him than I do. Once that connection was made, it was a wrap,” said Triple L, adding, “I built the rhythm from a real place. He heard it, he felt it, and the energy just matched. When two people are fighting for the same purpose, things can come together quickly.”

The resulting production is deliberately raw and forceful, combining the weight of the drums with a more hopeful melodic element.

“This isn’t soft music; this is warrior music,” he said. “You can hear the streets in it, but you can also hear the future. It was made to move speakers and move minds, bodies, and souls.”

At the heart of Keep On Fighting is a message of personal responsibility, resilience, and self-worth, particularly for young people.

“Stop making excuses. Man up. Do what needs to be done. Life is going to knock you down, but you don’t have to stay there,” he said. “To the youth, know your worth. You are not what the streets say you are. Keep on fighting. Diamonds are made under pressure.”

The producer said the decision to release the project independently reflects his wider vision of building from the ground up while maintaining ownership of his work.

“We’re not waiting for anybody to believe in us. We’re putting our own work out there and owning our masters. From the bottom to the top,” he said.

Distributed by VPAL, Triple L also sees Keep On Fighting as a progression in his development as a producer. While his earlier work focused heavily on rhythms and beats, he believes the new production represents a deeper understanding of how instrumentation can carry a message.

He believes the song’s universal theme will allow it to resonate well beyond Jamaica, pointing to the fact that struggle is something shared by people regardless of their background.

“Because everybody is fighting something. It doesn’t matter where you’re from. Everybody gets tired, but everybody is still here,” he said. “When they hear this song, they’re going to say, ‘That’s me.’ And if it stops even one young person from giving up, then we did our job.”

Triple L also credits his upbringing in Trench Town, a community synonymous with reggae’s history, as an important part of the perspective he brings to his production.

“I didn’t come from comfort. I came from the concrete jungle, from Trench Town, the home of reggae music,” he said.

While some producers may focus on following the latest sounds, Triple L said his priority is authenticity.

“A lot of producers are chasing trends. I’m chasing truth. I take my pain, I don’t complain, and I turn it into music. And I’m not doing it for fame. I’m doing it for the youth who need to know that they’re worth more,” he said.

World.title: Restrepo wants more opportunities for developing athletes
World.content:
Jamaica’s Shanoya Douglas (left) and Trinidad and Tobago’s Kayla Charles compete in the Under-20 Girls’ 200m heat during the Carifta Games at Kirani James Stadium in St George’s, Grenada, on Sunday, April 5. (Photo: Dennis Allen for @TTGameplan)

WORLD Athletics presidential hopeful Ximena Restrepo says providing consistent, high-level competition for athletes who are not yet at the top level of track and field should be a priority for the next Administration of the global governing body.

Restrepo, the first woman to serve as a vice-president of World Athletics and its current senior vice-president, was in attendance at the recent World Under-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon. She believes more can and should be done for athletes who do not have the resources to compete at top-level meets, most of which are staged in Europe.

The candidate, who is seeking to replace incumbent Sebastian Coe, believes a circuit that includes venues across the North American, Central American and Caribbean Athletic Association (NACAC) and South American regions would benefit athletes from those areas.

Restrepo, who attended the Carifta Games for the first time this year and was impressed with what she saw, said there are plenty of opportunities for junior athletes but questioned what happens after they leave school.

“There are competitions for the juniors. What happens with the seniors? What happens when the kids get out of school? That’s when things get tricky and not only on the islands; it happens all over the world,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Not every athlete who signs their first professional contract will be able to get into the more prestigious meets. While there will be local competition, Restrepo said more needs to be done to keep those athletes in the sport.

“That’s when we really need to find out how to keep those kids in the sport. What do we offer them?” she said.

While athletes such as three-time world-record holder Usain Bolt were able to remain in Jamaica while gaining access to top-level competition, Restrepo said that is not an option for everyone.

“In Jamaica you had Usain Bolt, he never left the island, and many of your athletes don’t really have to leave the island, but many others do. Which it’s okay. I mean, if they want to come to the US it’s their choice,” the former University of Nebraska sprinter said.

“But it has to be a choice, not something that they have to do because to survive because they can’t have something at home with their families or with their own coaches. So we have to create opportunities for our athletes so that they can choose where they want to go and what’s better for them. That’s at least the way I see it.”

Restrepo said although standards are good in the NACAC region, which includes the United States and Canada, there is still room for improvement.

“Well, I think everything can be always better. Even the best things can always get improved, so we have to keep working with the area together with World Athletics because it is a motor for World Athletics,” she said.

“I mean, sprinting in the Caribbean is just amazing. It’s the best in the world. You got excellent athletes. You got good weather, so you can train all year round. There are many good things that you do have in the Caribbean.”

In discussions with several presidents in the region, the former NCAA 400m champion and current Colombian national record-holder in the 200m and 400m said they discussed the need for more in-person coaching and refereeing courses, as well as greater access to meets for athletes unable to travel to Europe.

She said she had proposed the idea of a Caribbean Diamond League-style competition to provide more opportunities for those athletes.

“Why don’t we have a competition for our athletes in the Caribbean? You can bring people from other parts of the world as well,” she said. “It might sound crazy, but maybe we could do something. Maybe not for the top-top athletes, but flying to Europe is very expensive.”

While acknowledging that travel within the region is also expensive, Restrepo said the idea could work with the right financial backing.

“So it’s not an easy thing to do. But it takes money. But money can be found. I mean, if you have a good product and you know how to sell it. We could have something for those athletes that finish school. They can have a circuit in the islands that they can probably compete a little bit more,” she said.

“I may be wrong [but] it seems there is a lack of competition for that category of athletes.”

Restrepo said a South American circuit, with meets in Brazil, was another idea she was working on restoring.

“We are already talking Colombia, Brazil, Chile, Mexico may join us too. We are just talking about it because it’s difficult. We’re hoping to have three or four Continental Tour-Silver meets, that means a lot of points,” she said.

“You can go there and get points, not having to travel all the way to Europe with time change and if you go to Europe, it can’t be for just one meet, you need to go to different meets, and then you need to have a good manager to get you into the meets, which is complicated.”

“And what if you get injured, or if you need your coach, you have to travel with your coach, with your physio. I mean, that’s a lot of money. So we have to try to find middle ground solutions for many athletes because I think the top top athlete they have it fixed. They don’t have any problems. They have the money. They have good managers. They know they’re going to be entering into the big Diamond League competitions, they’re fine.”

“But we have a group of people that are B class that want to get to A class, and they’re still too young, they don’t have the experience. So, I would like to make it easier for them to get into that stage.”

World.title: ‘KEEP IT GOING’
World.content:
Rovman Powell (left) of Jamaica Kingsmen celebrates winning off Nathan Edwards (right) of Trinbago Knight Riders during their Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League match at Sabina Park in Kingston on Saturday night. (Photo: Randy Brooks/CPL T20)

Buoyed by a statement win over five-time champions Trinbago Knight Riders (TKR) on Saturday, Jamaica Kingsmen Captain Rovman Powell says his side will look to carry that momentum into tonight’s final home game.

The Kingsmen face St Kitts and Nevis Patriots (STKNP) at Sabina Park at 7:00 pm, with two crucial points on the line before heading on the road.

“If we can come up with another two points there, it would help us a lot…going on the road,” Powell said.

The Kingsmen opened their Caribbean Premier League (CPL) 2026 campaign with a commanding five-wicket win over TKR, chasing 183 with eight balls to spare.

It was a complete performance built on a blazing 93-run opening stand between Kirk McKenzie Jr (69 runs) and Reeza Hendricks (37 runs), and finished by experience in Powell (29 not out) and Andre Russell (27 runs).

The wheels wobbled briefly when Usman Tariq removed McKenzie on the last ball of the seventh over, then bowled Shayan Jahangir for two and had Hendricks caught next over.

Pollard had Keacy Carty caught for 11 to leave the Kingsmen at 126-4 in the 14th over, but Powell and Russell steadied things with a 48-run stand. Hasan Khan was three not out. Tarig finished with three for 21 from four overs.

Earlier, TKR, sent in to bat, posted 182-6 from 20 overs. Nicholas Pooran and Kieron Pollard each hit 44. Alex Hales made 29 and Colin Munro added 16. For the Kingsmen, Russell and Hunain Shah took two wickets each.

Powell credited the coaching staff for maintaining unity during the losing streak, noting that a day spent together without training helped the squad to jell.

“When we were 3-0 down, they didn’t go in their different corners and bicker. They stick together. We spent a nice day together, no training, just spend some time together and see if we can get to understand each other,” he said.

”When you form new teams, the players, they take a little bit of time to get jelly. Some of the guys are from Pakistan, South Africa, and across the Caribbean, and that jelling takes a little bit of time. And it’s just good to get a win in front of our own fans.”

Powell said that McKenzie was promoted to open the batting as a left-hander to counter spinner Akeal Hosein during the power play.

“We know Akeal Hosein would be the threat up top with the new ball, so we decided to send a left-hander to go and take him on and see how much he can get us in the powerplay.

“When chasing a score like that, with Trinidad having three quality spinners, you want to get a good start because you know in the middle overs when Sunil Narine takes the ball, it’s going to be difficult to hit,” Powell said.

He said that against TKR, he and Russell targeted the depth bowling late.

“When we started trying to play out Sunil Narine and Usman Tarig, you could hear the crowd coming down on myself and Russell. But at that point we have enough experience to know that is the game.

“You know, if one of them gets us out, then we’ll look stupid. So once we do, we try to push it as deep as possible because Trinidad’s weakness is their depth bowling,” Powell said.

Powell acknowledged the home fans as the “12th man”, thanking them for their support despite the initial losses and noting their role in the team’s momentum.

“We always believe that the fans are the 12th man…and credit has to be given to them. You can see they were cricket-thirsty, you know, and they came out and support us for the first three games. I wholeheartedly tell them thanks for that, you know, but we’re not done, you know, we still have one more game to go at home,” he said.

World.title: The Wedding Guest List Dilemma
World.content:
Couples should establish a preliminary guest count early, as it directly shapes their overall wedding budget.

Creating the wedding guest list sounds simple — until you actually have to do it. For today’s couples, weddings are becoming more personal, intentional and experience-driven. Many couples would rather host 80 people they genuinely love than invite 200 because tradition says they should. But weddings are also one of those rare occasions when family, culture, relationships and etiquette all collide. So how do you create a guest list that reflects your wedding while still respecting the traditions and people that matter? The answer isn’t necessarily to abandon tradition. It’s to modernise it.

Start With The Wedding You Can Actually Afford



Before names go onto a spreadsheet, establish your approximate guest count. Every additional guest potentially means another meal, chair, place setting, invitation, favour and portion of the bar budget. Depending on your wedding, it may also affect the size of the venue, transportation requirements and even the number of tables and floral arrangements required.

Your guest list and your budget therefore have to be developed together. A 100-person wedding isn’t simply a 75-person wedding with 25 extra chairs.

Create Your Non-Negotiable List First



Start with the people you cannot imagine celebrating without. For most couples, this includes immediate family, grandparents, closest friends and people who have played meaningful roles in their lives. Then create additional categories: Extended family, family friends, colleagues, parents’ friends and social acquaintances. This makes it much easier to see where your numbers are going before invitations become emotional decisions.

Yes, Parents Should Have Some Input

This is where modern wedding planning sometimes clashes with traditional etiquette. The wedding belongs to the couple, but marriage also represents the joining of families. Parents may have relatives, lifelong friends or important family relationships they genuinely believe should be acknowledged. Listen to them.

That doesn’t mean handing over half your guest list. Give each family an agreed number of invitations or ask them to submit a priority list. This allows parents to feel included without allowing the guest count to grow uncontrollably. If parents are making a significant financial contribution to the wedding, their expectations should ideally be discussed before the guest list is finalised.

Respect works both ways: Parents should understand the couple’s vision and limitations, and couples should recognise that some invitations carry family significance beyond their own personal relationships.

The Modern Rule: Relationship Over Obligation

There was once an expectation that if someone invited you to their wedding, you should invite them to yours. That’s no longer necessary. Perhaps their wedding was eight years ago and you haven’t spoken in five. Sometimes relationships change over time.

I have a rule of thumb: Ask yourself these two questions 1. If I weren’t getting married, would this person still be an active part of my life? 2. Do you think they will still be a part of your life in the next five years? Those questions can eliminate quite a few names. Your wedding shouldn’t become a reunion of everyone you’ve ever known simply because you’re worried someone might be offended.

But Don’t Forget Basic Courtesy

Being modern doesn’t mean abandoning good manners however. If you regularly socialise with a group of six friends, inviting five and excluding one will probably create unnecessary hurt. The same applies to very close family units. You don’t have to invite everyone from every social circle, but consider how your choices will feel from the other side. There is a difference between setting boundaries and being unnecessarily inconsiderate.

What About Plus-Ones?

This is one of the biggest guest-list questions. Generally, spouses, fiancés and established partners should be invited together — even if you haven’t personally met the partner. For single guests, however, you don’t necessarily have to offer everyone an unrestricted plus-one. If space and budget allow, it’s a lovely gesture, particularly for guests travelling alone or who won’t know many people at the wedding. Whatever rule you choose, try to apply it consistently.

Children or No Children?

An adults-only wedding is perfectly acceptable today, but communicate it clearly and graciously. You might choose to invite children only from immediate family or the wedding party. That’s also acceptable, provided the rule has some logic and isn’t being selectively applied to individual families. Give parents plenty of notice, particularly for a destination wedding where child-care arrangements may be more complicated.

Don’t Forget the Destination Wedding Reality

For destination weddings, the guest list requires another level of consideration. Inviting someone doesn’t mean they will automatically attend. Guests may need to purchase flights, book accommodation, take time away from work and possibly arrange childcare. Send save-the-dates early and avoid assuming who can or cannot afford to attend. Let guests make that decision for themselves. And please don’t invite someone simply because you believe they won’t come. They just might!

Be Careful With the B-List

Having a secondary list isn’t inherently wrong. Venues have capacities and couples have budgets.The problem comes when guests realise they were obviously an afterthought.

If you’re working with invitation rounds, send your first invitations early enough to receive responses before approaching the next group. Avoid sending a second wave suspiciously close to the wedding date unless circumstances genuinely changed. Nobody wants to feel like they were invited because somebody else cancelled.

Consider the People Who Have Been Part of the Journey



Sometimes couples become so focused on immediate friends that they overlook people who have genuinely contributed to their lives. The aunt who helped raise you. Your parents’ best friends who have known you since childhood. The mentor who helped shape your career. The family friend who has been present for every major milestone.

Tradition can sometimes remind us of something valuable: a wedding isn’t only about who you socialise with right now. It can also honour the people who helped you become who you are.

That doesn’t mean inviting everyone your parents have ever met. It means looking at your relationships with a little perspective.

And What About Co-workers?

You don’t have to invite the entire office. If colleagues have become genuine friends outside of work, invite them because of the friendship — not because you share an employer. If you’re inviting only a few people from a larger workplace, discretion is important. Wedding invitations don’t need to become lunchtime office announcements.

The Final Test

Before finalising your list, look at each name and ask: Do we genuinely want this person there? Is there an important family or cultural reason they should be included? Will excluding them create a significant and legitimate family issue? Are we inviting them because we want to — or purely because we feel guilty? Not every answer will be straightforward, and that’s okay.

Today’s couples should absolutely feel empowered to create weddings that reflect who they are. Smaller weddings, adults-only celebrations, limited plus-ones and carefully curated guest lists are all perfectly reasonable.

But in our desire to make weddings more personal, we shouldn’t lose the graciousness that has always been at the heart of good wedding etiquette.

Your wedding is your celebration, but it is also a moment shared with family and community.

The best guest lists find room for both.

Invite with intention. Set boundaries with kindness. Honour the relationships that deserve honouring. And when tradition still has meaning, don’t be afraid to keep it.

World.title: 10 interesting facts on the birthday of Marcus Garvey
World.content:
Marcus Garvey

On the 139th anniversary of the birth of Marcus Garvey, Jamaica’s first national hero, Observer Online shares some interesting facts about the late Pan-Africanist.

Garvey was born in St Ann’s Bay, St Ann in 1887. His message of black empowerment is the driving force of the Pan African movement he started in 1920 while living in New York, where he was a pillar of the Harlem Renaissance.

His teachings inspired many freedom fighters across the globe including Dr Martin Luther King Jr and Malcolm X, and recording artistes like Bob Marley and Burning Spear.

He died in London in June 1940 at age 52. Here are some interesting facts below.

1. Garvey’s parents, Malcus Mosiah Garvey Snr, a stone mason, and Sarah Jane Richards, a domestic worker, had 11 children. However, only Marcus Garvey and his elder sister Indiana lived to adulthood, with the other nine siblings dying in early childhood.

2. Garvey attended elementary school in Jamaica until age 14, and was thereafter instructed privately by tutors. As a young man, he had a talent for public speaking.

3. As a teen, Garvey migrated from St Ann to Kingston, where he worked as a printer and became involved in politics and trade unionism, leading a major print workers’ strike in 1908.

4. He published the short-lived political magazine, “The Watchman”, inspired by George William Gordon’s historical abolitionist paper. It folded after three issues.

5. As Garvey travelled internationally, he observed the poor living conditions and victimization of black people, compelling him to empower people of African descent.

6. On Emancipation Day in 1914, in Jamaica, he launched the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA), encouraging self-government for black people worldwide; self-help economic projects and protest against racial discrimination.

7. The first UNIA division was formed in New York in May 1917, and within a month, it had two million members across the US. By 1920, there were 1,100 chapters in 40 countries around the world.

8. Garvey launched the UNIA’s Black Star Line Steamship Corporation in New York in 1919, aimed at establishing an efficient mode of transportation, communication and trade among black people globally while enhancing the image and pride of black people.

9. Garvey had numerous enemies, including FBI director J Edgar Hoover and fellow black leader W.E.B. Du Bois, who opposed Garvey’s separatism and repatriation efforts. Du Bois and NAACP members organised the ‘Garvey Must Go’ campaign to have the Jamaican deported.

10. Marcus Garvey was twice married. His and his first wife, Amy Ashwood Garvey, divorced after three years of marriage. He and second wife, Amy Jacques Garvey, had two sons – Marcus Garvey Jnr and Julius Winston Garvey.

World.title: Defend truth, liberty
World.content:
Reverend Astor Carlyle (right) shakes hands with Governor General Sir Patrick Allen as Lady Allen (second right) and Chief of Defence Staff Vice Admiral Antonette Wemyss Gorman (left) look on at the end of Sunday’s church service commemorating 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension, Up Park Camp in St Andrew. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Jamaicans have been urged to summon the courage of a previous generation and stand firm in defence of truth and liberty just as men and women from this region answered the call to serve when World War II plunged the world into geopolitical turmoil and economic uncertainty.



Reverend Captain Astor Carlyle made the appeal on Sunday in his sermon during the service celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Royal Air Forces Association (RAFA) Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension inside the Jamaica Defence Force’s Up Park Camp headquarters in St Andrew.

According to RAFA, the service, held under the theme ‘80 years of service, sacrifice, and unity’, marks the commencement of a year of celebrations to mark its founding.

Referencing the first lesson — Isaiah 6:1-8, which tells of the prophet Isaiah seeing a vision of God, realising he is sinful, gets cleansed by a burning coal, and volunteers to serve God by saying, ‘Here am I. Send me!’ — Rev Carlyle said that in the time of Isaiah, Judah needed someone to shoulder the responsibility of being God’s representative during great confusion.

“Throughout the Bible, God asks questions, but there is one question from the lips of God that is very relevant for a day like this when we celebrate 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association; it is a question that we heard in the first scripture reading today: Whom shall I send? Who will go for us? And this was a question asked of the prophet Isaiah in a time that needed a Godly voice and a Godly presence to bring calm and consciousness to a nation in crisis,” Carlyle told the congregation of mostly ex-servicemen and women.

“This was a time of chaos, a time of complexity, a time of corruption, and when the young Isaiah stood in the presence of God and considered the grave need, he responded with five words, ‘Here am I, send me.’ Isaiah saw what was at stake, and without concern for himself, he answered in the affirmative,” Carlyle said.

“This is a picture of the kind of spirit with which our Caribbean service members engaged the desperate call from the allied forces in 1939. It was a time of geopolitical and economic instability. Dictators were emerging in Europe and Asia, threatening the fragile peace that the Treaty of Versailles sought to ensure. The Great Depression and the subsequent invasion of Poland required the allied forces to sound the rallying call, and with a spirit of duty and a sense of mission our Caribbean servicemen said ‘Here am I, send me.’ Some trained as pilots, some trained as navigators, some were ground crew under the British Commonwealth air training plan.

“They served in Europe, they served in North Africa, they served in the Mediterranean, they served in Asia. Many Jamaicans served with the Royal Air Force bomber command and fighter command, defending Britain during air raids and helping push back the Axis forces. These young men of the Caribbean faced grave danger, but not for fame or reward, they believed in freedom that was worth defending and they paid the ultimate sacrifice. That is why we celebrate their gallantry today,” Carlyle said.

He stated that the service Jamaicans gave during the war stands as a reminder that the call to duty is for the willing, and encouraged citizens to demonstrate a willingness to serve, just as the war veterans did.

“Isaiah displayed that spirit when God asked ‘Whom shall I send?’ He didn’t give excuses, he didn’t say I am not qualified enough or I have too many responsibilities, or I am too young or I am too old. He simply said, ‘Here I am, send me.’ That is the heart of a willing servant. God expects the same of you and me, He’s asking us that same question today. As our world shows signs of economic shocks and geopolitical uncertainty God is asking who is willing, who will stand for truth, who will serve?” Carlyle told the congregation.

Earlier, in her welcome, RAFA President Major (Retired) Johanna Lewin shared that the founding members of the organisation, formed on August 16, 1946, were a band of merry men who served in the Royal Air Force during World Ward II and did so with a deep sense of pride.

RAFA, she said, initially was for those who served in the war and returned home to Jamaica “to continue their camaraderie and visit the proverbial river — the bar”.

“They wanted to ensure that all was not forgotten and that the comradeship and shared sense of duty that they developed during the war years were persevered. How many of you are familiar with Colonel Reggie Chin, who was commanding officer of the Third Battalion for many years and who served with RAF during the war? How many of you are familiar with Michael Manley, former [Jamaica] prime minister, who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force during World War II? We could be here all day. It’s a long story and cannot be given justice here,” Lewin said.

She shared that RAFA started under a hut at one end of the airfield at the JDF Air Wing in Up Park Camp.

“We were offered three prime camp locations, but the one selected was what we know as Curphey Place in Swallowfield, the home of RAFA and the Jamaica Legion. The land was eventually given in perpetuity for the benefit of veterans. RAFA evolved and became more than just a means for these sassy World War II veterans to visit the ever-present river and chat and reminisce and sing about their experiences in Britain,” Lewin said.

“One of the early and major philanthropic works took place when the British charity… established Cheshire Homes, what we would term a hospice. RAFA was the first local entity to pledge $10,000, a tidy sum in those days, to build one of the units. Cheshire Homes is what we now know as the Mona Rehab. We were able to fund the original columbarium in Briggs Park and now the extension. RAFA has continued its tradition of raising funds and giving,” Lewin said.

World.title: German lawmakers call for EU sanctions on Israel’s Ben-Gvir over Gaza killing remarks
World.content:
“Ben-Gvir’s inhumane remarks can only be condemned,” Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson for the Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union parliamentary group, told POLITICO. “The EU should sanction him as a sign of the universal validity of human dignity and human rights.”

Hardt went further, saying he was convinced an Israeli government without Ben-Gvir or fellow far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich would bring Europe and Israel closer together.

Germany’s Social Democrats struck a similar tone. Adis Ahmetović, the party’s foreign policy spokesperson, said the two ministers had shocked international opinion well before their latest statements, and urged the German government to support sanctions against both.

The criticism extended across the political spectrum.

The Left’s Dietmar Bartsch called Ben-Gvir’s remarks “deeply inhumane,” and urged Berlin and Brussels to consider sanctions, including an entry ban. Markus Frohnmaier, the far-right Alternative for Germany party’s foreign policy spokesperson, said calling for the indiscriminate killing of people who posed no immediate threat crossed “a clear line.” Green Member of Parliament Marlene Schönberger branded Ben-Gvir a “far-right extremist” and said his comments were “deeply inhumane,” adding that they had “nothing whatsoever” to do with Israel’s right to defend itself and its citizens.

The statements mark a significant shift in Berlin. Germany has repeatedly pushed back against EU measures targeting Israel, including proposed sanctions on Ben-Gvir in June and, as recently as last month, restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

World.title: Andy Burnham ‘not embarrassed’ by exchange with Trump aide impersonator
World.content:
“All politicians are, you know, receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right,” Burnham said during a visit to Wolverhampton. “There was a minimal exchange of information of zero consequence, and it was quickly reported,” he added.

“I realized that this needed to be reported, and I did so. So I handled it in the right way,” he also said.

The incident has raised questions about potential national security vulnerabilities when it comes to the communications of senior politicians.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was among three Cabinet ministers whose numbers were found online by POLITICO on Monday.

Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary on Tuesday called for an inquiry into the Burnham message exchange, which he described as a “dangerous security breach.”

In a letter to the chair of the Intelligence and Security Committee, he wrote: “This is an unacceptable breach. The security of the Prime Ministers’ communications ought to be absolute priority — and yet it appears, in this case, that routine measures to guard against these kinds of breaches were not followed.”

Burnham would not say whether the government planned to change procedures in response to the dupe, but insisted that “the correct action has been taken here and in the U.S.”

World.title: France probes disinfo campaigns targeting 2027 election candidates
World.content:
Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal attend a campaign meeting of Renaissance on May 7, 2024. | Thomas Samson/AFP via Getty Images

Presidential contenders Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal were purportedly targeted by Russia-affiliated networks this summer.

PARIS — The Paris prosecutor’s office has launched an investigation into disinformation efforts targeting two prominent candidates in France’s upcoming presidential election, according to Agence France-Presse.

Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, two former prime ministers who are high-profile contenders for the 2027 race, were reportedly the subject earlier this summer of fake news reports posted on social media aimed at undermining their campaigns.

Fabricated videos posted on X that used branding from leading French news platforms claimed Philippe, who suffers from alopecia, was diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disease, while fake reports on X and TikTok alleged Attal had Parkinson’s disease and was using drugs.

World.title: Greece sabotages its own plans to reverse the brain drain of scientists
World.content:
In a statement published in May, Greece’s education ministry said the country’s finance ministry had decided to “remove the project during the review of Greece’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan.” It was later revealed that on the day the list of selected proposals was officially published, the government also delisted the program — but no one informed the applicants for 10 months.

“It was ultimately not possible to implement the project ‘Trust your Stars’ within the time frame set out by the RRF,” said an official from the education ministry. “For this reason, the project was removed, as part of a review of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan by the Council of the European Union.”

“As regards the funds linked to the actions in question, these were redirected to finance other actions undertaken by the RRF and the Education Ministry. Consequently, under no circumstances was there any loss of resources from the RRF,” added the official.

Shattered hopes

On July 15, Greece’s finance ministry issued a statement, saying it was trying to secure funds “to settle any outstanding financial obligations arising from legal commitments entered into at the time of the revocation of the program.”

While the statement rekindled hopes that a solution would be found, Hatzis argues that it was just a legal trick and that the education ministry has no legal commitment since no contracts were signed following the initial announcement of accepted proposals.

“What happened violates a fundamental principle, one that is sacrosanct in states governed by the rule of law: ‘reliance,’ the citizen’s legitimate trust in the state,” he said. “There may be no contractual liability, since we did not sign an agreement, but there is a political, moral and even legal obligation. Many young people turned down other offers or did not take up jobs elsewhere because they hoped they would be paid through the program.”

World.title: The Lib Dem dilemma: Cozy up to Burnham or strike out alone?
World.content:
A person familiar with Lib Dem Leader Ed Davey’s thinking, granted anonymity because their job does not authorize them to speak publicly, says the party hopes Burnham removes the “performative hostility” from Westminster.

“That style of politics really suits the populist parties, both on the left and the right, and it isn’t the sort of politics that we as Liberal Democrats want to do,” they argued.

But while not rocking the boat has landed well with Lib Dem MPs, there is still a call for a distinctive identity for the party in a highly competitive political environment, with Labour enjoying a “Burnham bounce” in the opinion polls on the left, and Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch’s personal brand on the up.

Duty of care

Davey — whose party enjoyed its best-ever result at the 2024 election but remains only just in double digits in national polls — has already made one big play in the Burnham era: being helpful on reforming social care.

The creaking social care system in England is a policy challenge governments of all stripes have failed to meet — leaving families with drained finances and cash-strapped local authorities plugging the gaps.

The Lib Dem leader, who cares for his disabled son, attended a virtual cross-party meeting after Burnham, whose own father is in a care home with Alzheimer’s, called for an open conversation on a fix.

World.title: New Expedia data shows autumn travel can still be more affordable than summer – if you know where to look
World.content:
Summer crowds will soon be fading, but the autumn travel bargain isn’t quite as guaranteed as it once was.

 

New data from Expedia shows that hotel prices are rising in some destinations this autumn but, in better news, other parts of Europe get noticeably less expensive once peak season ends.

From the Algarve and Greek islands to emerging hotspots in the Balkans, here are the European destinations where travellers can still find an autumn deal, plus the places seeing the biggest surge in interest.

Across much of the UK, Expedia data reveals that hotel prices are actually higher in the autumn than in the summer, with the largest increases in Birmingham and Liverpool, which are 30% and 20% higher respectively.

Outside of the UK, though, hotel rates tend to fall by an average of 7%.

In Albufeira and Faro in the Algarve, and Mykonos and Kos in the Greek Islands, rates are up to 30% lower when autumn comes, and the likes of Benidorm, Alicante and Istanbul are also less pricey in the -ber months – especially November.

“When you travel matters,” Melanie Fish, travel expert and spokesperson for Expedia, said.

“International stays on Expedia are, on average, 10% cheaper in November than in summer, making it the sweet spot for savvy travellers looking to unlock the best deals.”

One trick to finding a well-priced shoulder season trip is to plump for less obvious destinations which don’t tend to attract huge crowds in the autumn.

Expedia has revealed its fastest-growing autumn destinations, which are well worth looking at if you’re after an affordable trip which is relatively off the beaten track.

Annecy in France was in the top ten trending cities list Mmoka/Unsplash

Expedia’s trending autumn destinations

To establish which destinations are trending for next season, Expedia looked at searches made on Expedia.co.uk between April 13, 2026 to July 12, 2026 for travel between September 1, 2026 to November 30, 2026 and compared it to the same period in 2025.

Seven out of the top ten trending autumn destinations are in Europe, with a relatively little-visited country coming in first place.

Luxembourg, with a popularity of fewer than 700,000, is hugely trending, according to Expedia’s findings.

In fact, interest is surging by 470% among Britons, presumably seeking out city breaks in places not overrun with tourists.

In neighbouring France, searches for the pretty cities of Strasbourg and Annecy are up by 170% and 165% respectively, while Cortina d'Ampezzo in Italy, best known as a ski resort, has seen a rise of 115%.

Elsewhere in Europe, it seems as though travellers are opting for less established destinations for autumn breaks.

Sarandë in Albania (+110%), Budva in Montenegro (+85%) and Ljubljana in Slovenia (+80%) are in 8th, 9th and 10th places, which suggests autumnal travellers are keen to explore places fewer people have visited previously.
