According to the Azerbaijani authorities, the broadcasts contained calls for the violent overthrow of the country’s constitutional order, violations of its territorial integrity, terrorist activity and incitement of ethnic hatred.

The criminal case is being investigated under Articles 214-2, 281.2 and 283.2.1 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code. A court ordered the three men to be detained in absentia.

Excerpts from the broadcasts published by Azerbaijani media include remarks about a possible military operation against Baku, military pressure on Azerbaijan from the Caspian Sea and the use of physical violence against the country’s leadership. However, the Prosecutor General’s Office has not published full transcripts of the broadcasts, expert assessments or all the episodes on which the charges are based.

What do Uralov and Chadayev say?

The accused reject Baku’s allegations. Alexei Chadayev denied inciting ethnic hatred, saying that his criticism was directed not against the Azerbaijani people but against the country’s political leadership.

Semyon Uralov, for his part, described the Azerbaijani authorities’ decision as politically motivated. In subsequent Telegram posts, he continued to sharply criticise the political systems of post-Soviet countries, including the Azerbaijani authorities.

The response indicates that the case has moved beyond the legal sphere and become part of the broader information confrontation between the two countries.

‘International wanted list’ does not mean automatic arrest

The term “international wanted list”, used by Azerbaijani media, does not mean that a wanted person will automatically be arrested in another country.

Even if Interpol issues a Red Notice, it does not constitute an international arrest warrant. Each country decides whether to detain a wanted person in accordance with its own laws. In addition, Interpol’s constitution prohibits the organisation from intervening in matters of a political, military, religious or racial character.

The outcome of Baku’s request will therefore depend on the legal evidence submitted, as well as on how other countries assess the case — as a criminal prosecution or as a continuation of the political confrontation.

Ukraine factor

The latest escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations comes against the backdrop of the growing prominence of the Ukraine issue.

On 6 August, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov made his first official visit to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and visited Irpin. Azerbaijan reiterated its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying Azerbaijani gas to Ukraine.

Against this political backdrop, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko visited Baku on 16–17 August and met Ilham Aliyev. The presentation to Aliyev of a certificate naming him an honorary citizen of Irpin could be perceived in Moscow as a symbolic political gesture.

There is no evidence confirming a direct link between these developments and Hasanov’s deportation. However, the Azerbaijani leadership’s increasingly open articulation of a position on Ukraine that differs from Moscow’s fits into the broader picture of growing discontent in Russian political circles.

New mechanisms of mutual pressure

One notable change in relations between Baku and Moscow over the past two years has been the increasingly active use of law-enforcement and administrative mechanisms in the context of their political confrontation.

Russia has applied citizenship and migration laws, as well as criminal legislation, against members of the Azerbaijani diaspora. Azerbaijan, in turn, has used criminal prosecution mechanisms against individuals linked to Russian media over statements that Baku regards as posing a threat to the country.

This does not in itself mean that the legal arguments put forward by either side are unfounded. However, the fact that such legal measures are being taken against the backdrop of political crises in bilateral relations inevitably raises questions about their selective application and possible use for political purposes.

Where are relations heading?

At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: Prosecutor says former deputy economy minister Mikautadze gave bribe to ex-security chief Liluashvili
World.content:
Corruption cases in Georgia

Prosecutor Mariam Berdzenishvili said former deputy economy minister Romeo Mikautadze was supposed to go to the State Security Service and personally hand over the money to its former head, Grigol Liluashvili. She said the money was delivered to Liluashvili’s office. Berdzenishvili told reporters this before a court hearing in the case against Grigol Liluashvili.

According to the prosecutor, Mikautadze, who testified as a witness in the case, told the court that he underwent a security check and other required procedures when he entered the State Security Service (SSS) building. He then went to Liluashvili’s office.

Berdzenishvili said the investigation also has other evidence supporting the accuracy and reliability of the information provided by Mikautadze. In particular, investigators questioned a businessman who, according to the prosecutor, gave the court virtually the same account as Mikautadze.

She said the investigation requested data from the relevant companies covering the period when Mikautadze allegedly handed the money to Liluashvili. Berdzenishvili said an analysis of mobile phone data and internet traffic showed that the two men were in the same place at the same time.

“The prosecution also requested documents relating to the alleged handover of the bribe,” she added.

The prosecutor said the case contains direct evidence supported by other materials, and that there are no objective grounds to question its credibility.

Berdzenishvili said the defence argument that no third parties were present when the money changed hands was not significant to the case. According to her, demands for and payments of bribes generally do not take place in public or in the presence of large numbers of people.

Asked whether Mikautadze went directly to the SSS and handed the money to Liluashvili, Berdzenishvili replied: “Yes. According to the witness, that is what happened.”

The prosecutor said the investigation had also questioned other people who had previously visited Liluashvili. According to their testimony, the procedure for receiving visitors was not always the same.

“The witness also described how he entered the relevant office after undergoing a security check and other procedures. Other people who had previously visited Grigol Liluashvili were also questioned about how they entered the building. Security staff recorded the entry procedure and noted that it did not always involve issuing a pass, a search and so on. In other words, the defendant himself decided how visitors would enter his office,” Berdzenishvili said.

According to her, these circumstances and other factual evidence in the case support the reliability of the information Mikautadze provided to the court.

Berdzenishvili said Mikautadze told the businessmen that the money was being handed over in the interests of the state. According to the prosecutor, one of the businessmen also confirmed this.

“According to the witness, he told the businessmen that this was being done in the interests of the state. One of the businessmen also confirmed this during questioning. They presented the payment as something that served the state’s interests, although this was merely a formal justification. Of course, it was clear to everyone involved that it did not actually serve any state interest,” the prosecutor said.

Berdzenishvili also confirmed that, according to the investigation, Mikautadze brought the money to Liluashvili’s office in a bag.

“Yes, he had the money in his bag. As for his presence in the building, we questioned a security guard who confirmed that he saw Romeo Mikautadze, for example, on the same floor,” she said.

Journalists also asked the prosecutor whether Romeo Mikautadze could face charges, since he was the person who delivered the money to Liluashvili.

According to Berdzenishvili, the involvement of many people in the case is clear. However, authorities cannot classify a person’s actions as a crime until they launch criminal proceedings against that individual.

“I cannot call it a crime in advance until criminal proceedings have been launched against a particular person. I cannot classify a specific action as a crime — even in the case of Grigol Liluashvili. I am speaking based on the standard of reasonable suspicion. In general, if the case confirms that standard, criminal proceedings may be launched,” she said.

As for Mikautadze providing information to investigators, the prosecutor described it as cooperation. She said the defence was wrong to argue that Mikautadze was cooperating with investigators only to receive certain benefits and that such cooperation itself constituted a crime.

The prosecutor also did not rule out bringing criminal charges against Romeo Mikautadze in the future if investigators find sufficient grounds to do so.

“I did not rule that out. I simply described the situation that the defence presents as some kind of special case. I want to stress that the authorities will address the actions of all those involved, the decisions they made and the extent of their cooperation with the investigation within the framework of the law and justice,” Mariam Berdzenishvili said.

Background

Romeo Mikautadze is a former deputy economy minister. The State Security Service arrested him on 21 June 2025. According to the agency, Mikautadze faced charges of abuse of office and laundering millions of lari in illicit proceeds.

The case initially focused on corruption allegations against Mikautadze. In March 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison. Mikautadze also testified as a witness in the case against Grigol Liluashvili. The prosecution considers his testimony one of its key pieces of evidence.

Grigol Liluashvili headed the State Security Service from 2019 until April 2025. He left his post on 2 April 2025.

Liluashvili was arrested on 23 December 2025 after appearing for questioning at the prosecutor’s office. Investigators accuse him of receiving a particularly large bribe as part of a group acting in a prior agreement. According to the case file, the charges involve several episodes, including two linked to Romeo Mikautadze.

The charges against Liluashvili concern receiving a particularly large bribe. The relevant article carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

Corruption cases in Georgia

World.title: School uniforms return to Georgia’s public schools: what you need to know
World.content:
School uniforms in Georgia

Boys will wear jackets like these to school. Photo: Educational Resources

From the new school year, school uniforms will become compulsory for pupils from first to sixth grade in Georgia’s public schools. Boys will wear dark blue trousers and jackets, while girls will wear jackets made from the same material and skirts. The uniforms were made in China and consist mainly of synthetic materials.

The Education Ministry spent more than 45 million lari on the uniforms (approximately $17,226,540,000 — JAMnews). However, the uniforms will not be free for pupils, as parents will have to buy them from the government. Only children from socially vulnerable families will receive free sets.

The ministry says standardised uniforms will reduce social differences and strengthen pupils’ sense of belonging to their schools. However, some parents question the need for compulsory school uniforms. Their main concern is whether it makes sense to prioritise uniforms when more pressing problems with school infrastructure, safety and food remain unresolved.

Questions have also been raised about the quality and comfort of the uniforms. How comfortable will they be for young children? Will they be able to fasten the buttons and zips themselves? Will they be too hot in summer or too cold in winter?

Why has the school uniform become compulsory? How safe is the fabric used to make it for children’s health? Why did the government choose a Chinese company when Georgia also has a developed textile industry? What exactly will standardised uniforms change in Georgia’s troubled education system?

Why has the ministry decided to bring back school uniforms?

In September, six-year-old Ilia will begin a new stage of his life — he is starting school. Ilia attended kindergarten, but adapting to a new environment and stricter discipline will still be a challenge for him.

Ilia will face another challenge — running and playing during breaks in a polyester jacket and tight-fitting trousers.

“My son is used to wearing clothes made of cotton or wool with a small amount of elastane. Until he was six, he did not even wear jeans because they were not stretchy enough. I do not know how he will be able to run around in this jacket during school activities. And I wonder whether it will even stay on him. I doubt that restrictive clothing, against the backdrop of the stress of adapting to school, will help a child develop a sense of belonging to school life,” says Ilia’s mother, Taya Maharashvili.

Taya plans to contact the Education Ministry and demand stronger justification for making school uniforms compulsory:

“I have never opposed introducing a dress code. I believe it is important to dress appropriately in educational and professional environments, and children should learn this from an early age. However, the uniform proposed by the ministry is unacceptable.”

Introducing school uniforms for pupils in the lower grades of public schools is one element of a planned large-scale education reform. Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the measure on 2 December 2025 during a presentation of the National Concept for General Education Reform.

“School uniforms will help create an environment focused on learning and foster a sense of belonging to the educational institution. They will also reduce visible differences in pupils’ socio-economic backgrounds,” Mikanadze said.

School uniforms were compulsory in Georgia in the past. In Soviet schools, pupils wore dark brown, black or blue uniforms with white aprons. In independent Georgia, only some private schools require uniforms, although parents there have also complained about the quality of the fabric.

Polyester, viscose and elastane — what materials are used to make the clothes?

School uniform design. Photo: Education Ministry

The appearance, colour and quality of the school uniforms were determined entirely by the state. The boys’ uniforms will be plain dark blue, while the girls’ uniforms will feature a checked pattern. The state emblem will appear on the left side of the jacket.

The uniforms are made mainly from synthetic materials: 72% polyester, 25% viscose and 3% elastane.

The jackets will also have polyester lining. According to ministry documents, only the skirts will have cotton lining.

The uniforms can be washed at 40°C and ironed at 110°C. Bleach is prohibited, as is ironing the emblem or dry-cleaning the garment.

The school uniform set will include a jacket and trousers for boys, and a jacket and skirt (or a jacket and trousers) for girls.

“First of all, this uniform is uncomfortable. It reminds me of a situation where a paediatric dietitian insists that a child eat vegetables, only for the child to spit them out. I have the feeling that the ministry employs people who have no idea what children and childhood are like,” Taya says.

One uniform set will cost 95 lari. Some pupils will receive it for free.

Trousers and skirts will cost 25 lari, while a jacket will cost 45 lari. A set may include a jacket and two pairs of trousers, or a jacket, trousers and a skirt. As a result, one school uniform will cost parents 95 lari.

Most parents say one set will not be enough for a child to wear throughout the week. Pupils will also need a white shirt or T-shirt under the uniform, which parents will have to buy separately.

Pupils from socially vulnerable families will receive uniforms free of charge. This applies to families registered in the Unified Database of Socially Vulnerable Persons with a rating score below 65,001.

Children in state care or foster families, as well as those living in family-type homes or shelters for children without parental care, will also receive uniforms free of charge.

Ukrainian pupils who have been living and studying in Georgia since the start of the war will also receive school uniforms free of charge.

Is the uniform fabric safe? What should parents do if their child has an allergy or skin condition?

Third-grader Sandro has urticaria and allergic dermatitis. That is why his mother, Sopho, who is raising him alone, pays close attention to the quality of his clothes.

“My son is at school from 9:30am until 6pm, and I am concerned about everything: the quality, comfort and presence of allergens,” says Sopho Trapaidze.

Polyester, the material used for the uniforms, is widely used in the textile industry because it is durable and inexpensive. However, doctor Eka Kvirkvelia notes that the material is not suitable for everyone and is not hypoallergenic for all people. In some cases, it can contribute to overheating, increased sweating and skin irritation.

“True hypoallergenicity depends not only on the composition, but also on the fabric’s breathability, the chemical composition of dyes, production standards and the lining material. It is also important to understand that ‘international practice’ does not mean there is a single standard: different countries use different approaches. Nevertheless, natural fabrics or materials with a high cotton content are often preferred for primary school pupils,” she wrote on social media.

According to her, assessing the quality of school uniforms should rely on specific indicators, such as the percentage of each component, dermatological test results and data on children’s safety, rather than broad claims such as “hypoallergenic”.

Taya Maharashvili has also begun looking at practices in other countries. Polyester is used in schools in some developed countries, but there is one important detail:

“The percentage of polyester in our school uniforms is higher than in those countries. In addition, such countries more often introduce a dress code rather than a uniform. How the fabric has been treated and whether it meets safety standards are also important. They say these factors were taken into account when the Georgian school uniform was designed. However, the public should demand more reliable information supported by evidence, such as expert assessments and so on.”

Education Ministry says exceptions will be allowed

Parents are already demanding additional evidence from the Education Ministry that the fabric meets safety and quality standards. They are also calling on doctors to help address the issue.

“We demand a change in the fabric used for school uniforms. Synthetic clothing is harmful to children’s health,” Tamuna Gagnidze writes.

Dozens of parents have left comments under her post making similar demands. Many say they do not intend to dress their children in the uniforms.

“My child cannot wear polyester: he has atopic dermatitis, and contact with this material makes his skin worse. I absolutely do not want the school uniform to cause bleeding wounds on his skin,” says Hatuna Laghadze in a comment.

Sopho Trapaidze also does not plan to buy a new uniform for her son Sandro. She plans to make it herself — in the same style and colour, but from higher-quality material.

The Education Ministry says it will take into account cases where pupils have officially confirmed medical contraindications.

The Georgian Law on General Education regulates such cases. Article 19¹, paragraph 3, states that “a primary school pupil may be exempted from the obligation to wear a school uniform on health grounds based on a written agreement with the Ministry of Education”.

The ministry says such cases will be considered individually. Parents will need to provide the school with the relevant medical certificate. The pupil will still have to follow the established dress code.

What happens if a parent does not put their child in a school uniform?

School uniforms are compulsory. The ministry has placed particular emphasis on this point.

“Will they (officials — JAMnews) dress their own children in clothes made from this fabric?” This is the most common question in school groups and social media discussions about the uniforms.

“What happens if I do not put this uniform on my child? Will they be banned from going to school?” one parent asks in the comments.

“I have three school-age children. I am not going to buy it either. I consulted lawyers, and no one has the right to create problems for children because of this,” another parent replies.

When presenting the new uniforms, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze said that if parents refuse to use them, the school may address the issue through educational and disciplinary measures. The law does not specify which sanctions schools can impose.

The ministry says schools will consider each refusal on an individual basis. Each school will be able to find its own solution based on its internal rules.

What is known about the Chinese company making Georgia’s school uniforms?

School uniform production process. Photo: Educational Resources LLC

All matters related to the logistics of the school uniforms are handled by Educational Resources LLC, a department established within the Education Ministry in March 2026.

The ministry initially planned to manufacture the uniforms in Georgia. It considered using sewing workshops at state vocational colleges.

On 3 April 2026, the ministry announced a market study to procure the school uniforms. On 29 April, Educational Resources requested government approval to use a simplified procurement procedure. However, on 14 May, it emerged that the company initially selected did not meet the ministry’s requirements. The ministry had to restart the market study.

In June, the ministry signed a contract with Glory Textile Industry LLC to supply the school uniforms through direct negotiations, without a tender. The Education Ministry opted for direct negotiations to save time, as it needed to secure the uniforms and have them delivered before the start of the new school year.

Glory Textile Industry was registered in Georgia on 10 March 2026. Its sole owner and director is Chinese citizen Liu Xiaolin. The company received the order to manufacture the school uniforms just two months after its establishment and signed a 45.66 million lari contract with the Georgian government.

The company must deliver 1,801,000 items of clothing to Georgia between 25 August and 30 November:

Girls’ jackets — 292,000;

Boys’ jackets — 308,000;

Girls’ trousers — 438,000;

Boys’ trousers — 616,000;

Skirts — 146,000;

Long skirts — 1,000.

The uniforms are being made in China’s Jiangsu province at the Eton Kidd factory, which is operated by the SUMEC group.

Eton Kidd is a major Chinese school uniform brand. According to its official website, the company was founded in 2009. It works with more than 3,400 schools across 31 provincial-level administrative divisions, manufacturing and supplying school uniforms.

According to official information, SUMEC is an important subsidiary of the China National Machinery Industry Corporation (SINOMACH) and belongs to a group of state-owned enterprises directly under the central government of China.

Glory Textile Industry plans to deliver the school uniforms to Georgia in three stages:

Stage I — 301,000 items — by 25 August 2026;

Stage II — 600,000 items — by 15 October 2026;

Stage III — 900,000 items — by 30 November 2026.

First batch of uniforms arrives in Georgia. Where can parents get them?

The first batch of school uniforms has already arrived in Georgia. According to Educational Resources, the quantity is sufficient for first-graders.

The uniforms are currently being sorted into sets. Sales will begin on 1 September and continue until 14 September.

First batch of school uniforms. Photo: Educational Resources LLC

In the coming days, the uniforms will be distributed to major cities and regions. The authorities will also announce where parents can buy them. Parents will pay for the uniforms by cashless payment.

Uniforms for pupils in grades 2-6 will arrive later and will be distributed in two stages, on 15 October and 30 November.

This means pupils in grades 2-6 will not have uniforms in September. At the start of the school year, parents will have to buy regular clothes and purchase the uniforms later.

Will school uniforms change anything in Georgia’s education system?

The government is spending 45.66 million lari on school uniforms, saying they will help reduce social inequality. Meanwhile, Georgian schools still do not provide free meals.

According to a 2023 study by Georgia’s National Statistics Office, with support from UNICEF, only 27% of children aged 6 to 17 eat at school every day. Meanwhile, 34.9% do not eat at all during the school day. Among children from low-income families, the figure reaches 44.9%.

The same study found that 83.2% of parents believe schools should provide children with meals during the school day. In some Georgian schools, particularly in the regions, children cannot even buy food because the schools have no canteens.

Against the backdrop of these and other problems, school uniforms appear to be the least pressing issue facing Georgia’s public schools.

“I cannot support spending such a large amount of money on uniforms when schools have yet to address basic problems with toilets, canteens and the quality of education,” says Ana Gvaladze.

“We called the ministry 80 times to get the problem with the toilets at School No. 161 resolved,” adds Sopho Trapaidze.

Taya, who has been studying education issues in depth, says building a school culture is a complex process and involves much more than a set of behavioural rules:

“Schools face many problems today, from poor infrastructure and failures to meet health and hygiene standards to a lack of an emotionally safe environment for children. Children attend dull, grey schools. Sometimes a school has just one teacher, who provides the support that the education system as a whole should provide. So school culture cannot be strengthened through uniforms alone. Likewise, in such an unhealthy environment — and given the problems with crime in the country — uniforms cannot stop bullying.”

Taya notes that bullying does not actually start because of clothing.

“Clothing is just an excuse. If a bully is looking for a victim, they can pick on someone’s height, weight, glasses, shoes, bag or even pen. Uniforms cannot hide social differences. And most importantly, when the minister talked about school culture and a sense of belonging, did he forget that a child who is hungry because their school has no canteen will not develop any sense of belonging?”

Hundreds of thousands of Georgian schoolchildren will start the new academic year in “impoverished” conditions, in buildings that are not suitable for proper education. In recent years, hundreds of schools across the country have been demolished, while construction on many replacements has yet to begin.

School uniforms in Georgia

World.title: Former Georgian PM Irakli Garibashvili accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail
World.content:
Former PM accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail

Jailed former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has accused Georgian Dream honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili and the current government of blackmail.

In a statement released from prison on 17 August 2026, the former prime minister claimed he was being pressured to plead guilty to new corruption charges and permanently withdraw from politics at Ivanishvili’s demand. It is the first time that a former close ally of Ivanishvili has openly spoken out against the founder of the ruling party.

Plea deal ultimatum and plan to quit politics

A photograph of a printed letter dated 17 August was posted on the Facebook pages of Garibashvili and his wife, Nunuka Tamazashvili. Only four paragraphs of the letter were made public. It is unclear who wrote the letter or how it was delivered.

According to the published document, the government is offering the former prime minister a compromise. Under the proposed terms, Garibashvili would have to plead guilty to a new corruption-related charge.

The letter sets out the proposal in detail:

“They are offering me the option of pleading guilty in one case, where everything would be arranged by agreement, including a confession, witness signatures and so on. They are offering a plea bargain while retaining the same five-year sentence: that is, as it has been explained to me, the sentences would be combined, but the final term would remain five years.”

According to the document, a corruption conviction would serve as a form of “insurance” for the government, aimed at preventing the former prime minister from returning to politics in the future.

Two options and a political condition

The published letter refers to investigations into several cases. Its author suggests that these could result in corruption charges.

The text outlines two possible courses of action for Garibashvili. The first would involve continuing to contest the case in court.

“Let’s discuss this seriously and see it through to the end,” the document says.

The second option is presented as a compromise. According to the letter, Garibashvili would plead guilty in one of the cases, with the details agreed in advance:

“Let’s plead guilty in one case, where everything will be arranged by agreement: a confession, witness signatures and so on.”

The document also says that a new plea deal would not increase the five-year prison sentence already imposed on Garibashvili. The sentences would be combined, leaving the overall term unchanged at five years.

However, the proposal comes with a political condition.

“After leaving, you cannot engage in politics. If it is decided to ‘renege on the agreements’, then the corruption charges that will be brought will serve as an insurance mechanism, preventing even the thought of returning to politics,” the document says.

The authenticity of the letter has not been independently verified, and its author remains unknown. There is also no confirmation that new cases are in fact being prepared against Garibashvili.

Garibashvili’s first open confrontation with Ivanishvili

This marks Irakli Garibashvili’s first public confrontation with Bidzina Ivanishvili. For many years, Garibashvili was regarded as one of his most loyal political allies.

He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister, first from 2013 to 2015 and again from 2021 to 2024.

Garibashvili was sentenced under a plea agreement reached on 12 January 2026. He was given a five-year prison term and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated from him.

The case concerned the laundering of illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. Garibashvili is currently serving his sentence in a prison in Rustavi.

The new statement means that the former prime minister himself is now linking possible further legal action against him to demands that he stay out of politics. However, the material made public so far presents only Garibashvili’s version of events.

Response from MP Irma Inashvili, named in letter

The letter published by Garibashvili mentions MP Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze. According to the text, they — along with “supporters like them” and campaigns on social media — have raised suspicions.

“Supporters such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili, as well as campaigns organised on social media, have raised very serious suspicions and caused us tangible harm,” the document says.

Inashvili denied any involvement in organised campaigns. She said Irakli Garibashvili was her friend, but that she expressed her views publicly and independently.

“I have never planned or conducted any campaigns on social media; I don’t need such campaigns — I already express my views openly in my own name!” Inashvili wrote.

She said Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze was the main target of her criticism.

“I expose Kobakhidze and fight against him,” Inashvili said.

Opposition says Garibashvili being politically neutralised

Opposition figures have described Garibashvili’s letter as a sign of an internal conflict within the government. Their comments amount to political assessments and do not independently corroborate the circumstances described in the letter.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the contents of the letter pointed to a political motive behind Garibashvili’s imprisonment.

“Ivanishvili’s bargaining with Garibashvili — ‘I will punish you even more severely unless you give me guarantees that you will leave politics for good’ — confirms that the motive for his arrest is neither to punish a corrupt official nor to fight corruption in general, nor does it serve any public or state interest. It serves Bidzina’s personal political interests,” Gvaramia wrote.

He also qualified his comments by noting that the authenticity of the letter had not been established. Gvaramia particularly highlighted what he described as an attempt to politically neutralise Garibashvili.

Levan Samushia, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, linked the statement to the country’s current system of governance. He said any potential threat against Garibashvili’s family warranted a legal response.

“It is clear that Garibashvili is speaking about a possible, alleged threat to his family. This is an issue that requires particular attention and, naturally, provides grounds for launching an investigation,” Samushia said.

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, said he preferred to wait for further information before reaching a definitive conclusion. Nevertheless, he linked the developments to an internal conflict within Georgian Dream.

“The situation appears alarming because it concerns his family, and at this point clarity is the best means of protecting him and his loved ones,” Sichinava said.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, described Garibashvili’s case as a warning to current government figures.

“Garibashvili’s case should be learnt by heart by Ivanishvili’s current servants, officials and representatives of the financial sector who justify the government,” Dekanoidze wrote.

Government silent as questions remain unanswered

At the time of writing, reports about Garibashvili’s allegations had not appeared on the websites or Facebook pages of the pro-government Imedi and Rustavi 2 television channels.

Government representatives have yet to respond publicly to the central allegation. They have not said whether Bidzina Ivanishvili had any involvement in sending the letter to Garibashvili. It also remains unclear whether any new investigations into the former prime minister are under way.

Background: From alliance to prison

For many years, Irakli Garibashvili was regarded as one of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest political allies. He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister.

On 24 October 2025, Garibashvili was charged with laundering illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. A plea agreement was reached on 12 January 2026, under which the former prime minister was sentenced to five years in prison and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated. He has since been serving his sentence at a penitentiary facility in Rustavi.

Legal proceedings against former senior figures in the ruling team were preceded by internal party disagreements and arrests of officials from various state agencies. There have also been reports of investigative measures involving members of Garibashvili’s family.

The developments suggest that the power struggle within Georgian Dream has entered an increasingly acute phase.

World.title: Jailed former Pakistan PM Imran Khan moved to hospital over health concerns
World.content:
Pakistan's Supreme Court has ordered former prime minister Imran Khan be moved to hospital from jail, meeting a longstanding demand of his party and family, who had raised concerns about his health.

Cricketer-turned-politician Khan, 73, has been in jail in the garrison town of Rawalpindi since August 2023, convicted in a string of cases that he says were politically driven following his ouster in 2022.

His sons repeatedly expressed concern regarding his deteriorating health last year, with his lawyers saying he had lost significant vision in his right eye while in prison.

"Mindful of the fundamental right, we are issuing this order to ensure health and safety of the prisoner," said Justice Shahid Waheed, head of the three-judge bench that heard the petition.

The court directed that Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital in the capital Islamabad within 48 hours and remain there until September 16, Khan's spokesperson Naeem Haider Panjutha said on X.

A judge ordered supporters of the former Pakistani prime minister stay away from the hospital he has been taken to. (Reuters: Fayaz Aziz)

It also ordered the creation of a medical panel for his treatment, including a cardiologist, general medicine specialist, eye specialist and Khan's personal physician.

Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party welcomed the order, saying it should be implemented "immediately, fully, and without delay".

"We wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much," PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari said.

The party also appealed to its members and Khan's supporters not to gather outside the hospital, in accordance with the court's order.

No reaction from government

There was no reaction from the government to the court order and the information and interior ministries did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

Khan's younger son, Kasim, said his health was "all that mattered".

"We hope the government adheres to the court orders … allows calls and issues our visas to Pakistan simply so we can come and see him," he said in a statement shared with Reuters.

Thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have taken to the streets in recent years to protest his imprisonment. (AP: Irtisham Ahmed )

Kasim and his older brother Sulaiman — raised in Britain after Khan's divorce from their mother, British socialite and filmmaker Jemima Goldsmith — have not seen their father since 2022 in the absence of a visa.

Since he lost power in a no-confidence vote, Khan has faced multiple cases, including over state gifts and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. Some convictions have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.

Khan's initial arrest in May 2023 sparked protests that saw hundreds of people attacking state buildings and rampaging through military installations.

His supporters have similarly taken to the streets on several occasions in the years since to demand his release.

Cricket greats from around the world, including from across the border in rival India, demanded better treatment for Khan in February, expressing "deep concern" about his prison conditions.

The government had denied allegations of mistreatment.

PTI won power in 2018 and retains a large support base across key provinces but was stripped of its election symbol ahead of the 2024 vote.

Its candidates, who were forced to contest as independents, won the most seats in the election but fell short of the majority needed to form a government.

Reuters

World.title: Government to crack down on super switching schemes
World.content:
Unlicensed telemarketers that cold call and make unsolicited approaches to convince people to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino will appear at the National Press Club today and announce a suite of reforms to better protect Australians from falling victim to operators that rob them of their retirement savings.

The reforms follow the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian funds that saw 12,000 people lose more than $1 billion in retirement savings, and which exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's almost $4.5 trillion retirement savings pool.

Currently, people might go on Facebook and click an ad that looks innocent like "Find Your Lost Super" or "Check Your Super", but then gives permission for a telemarketer, also known as a "lead generator", to contact them and suggest they connect with a financial adviser to switch their super.

Mr Mulino said, under the changes, in order to be able to advertise, these lead generators would need to be licensed.

Daniel Mulino will present superannuation reforms at National Press Club. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

It stops short of the outright ban on advertising that some consumer groups have been calling for.

The assistant treasurer said there would be "exceptions" to protect advocacy, educational and employment communications.

Deep flaws in Australia's $4.3 trillion system exposed The collapses of the First Guardian and Shield schemes have exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's $4.3 trillion superannuation sector.

"These reforms are designed to disrupt some of the most damaging business models operating in the system today," Mr Mulino said.

"They target the point at which consumers are first exposed to harm and reduce the ability of bad actors to gain access to consumers in the first place."

Mr Mulino said he also wanted to "strengthen the anti‑hawking regime to enhance consent requirements, limit the existing financial advice exemption to existing client relationships and strengthen penalties for breaches".

That would require licensees "to take reasonable steps to ensure lead generation activities comply with relevant regulatory and legal requirements".

Super telemarketers lure investors in

Michael Johnson is one of thousands of investors who lost his retirement savings, along with his wife, Caroline, when First Guardian collapsed in April 2025.

They each had separate superannuation accounts with retail funds, but in October 2020 moved about $500,000 of their super from APRA-regulated funds into one joint self-managed superannuation fund (SMSF).

Michael Johnson and his wife lost $500,000 of their retirement savings. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mr Johnson said he decided to switch his super after seeing an  on Facebook, and then being contacted by a lead generator, who eventually put them onto financial advisers at United Global Capital (UGC).

ASIC to review super 'lead generators' ASIC is investigating whether lead generators are complying with their legal obligations when suggesting people switch their retirement savings into less-regulated investment schemes.

"It was just like other ads you see for changing your health insurance or your car insurance, and it said, 'Do a health check on your super,'" he said.

That call from the telemarketer quickly led to him connecting with financial advisory firm UGC, which convinced him and his wife to move all their super and invest it wholly in the First Guardian Master Fund.

UGC entered liquidation in August 2024 and ASIC cancelled the advisory firm's Australian Financial Services Licence (AFSL) in July 2024.

The primary adviser from UGC involved was contacted for comment but did not respond.

Mr Johnson said the financial advisers "were very convincing", but that had the government regulated lead generators before he and his wife switched their super, "we wouldn't have gone in at all".

Telemarketers, also known as lead generators, contact people after the click on social media ads and give their contact details. (iStock: Tero Vesalainen)

"Part of how this worked was a remarkably large number of people signing up at the same time," Mr Johnson said.

" The operators … constructed a scheme that was based on getting lots of people in quickly, grabbing that money and then going home and then disappearing with it. "

Mr Johnson said at the time he invested, First Guardian was described to the couple as a "diversified" investment vehicle.

He didn't realise anything was wrong until it was too late.

Proposed levy could cost self-managed super funds The assistant treasurer is looking to revamp funding for the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, saying that large super funds, as well as people with self-managed super funds (SMSFs), could be asked to chip in.

"It was devastating," Mr Johnson told ABC News.

"We're approaching retirement. Caroline was looking at reducing her work hours. We wanted to be able to retire and keep our current lifestyle."

Mr Johnson said the couple now did not know how they could financially manage.

"It looks like we will be needing to have a government pension and the whole point of having compulsory superannuation is that you don't need [to do] that," he said.

" It's impacted our mental health. That impacts our physical health. It's made life seem much harder. "

Call for social media companies to take down 'harmful' ads

Super Consumers CEO Xavier O'Halloran supports the ban on unlicensed cold calling, but wants to see obligations on social media platforms to take down harmful ads.

ASIC warns on online trading platforms A review of nine online trading companies finds several are encouraging Australians to jump on "complex" deals, putting them at risk of major losses.

He said that through lead generators, consumers' details then got sold on to a financial advisor "where you're put into really a train towards selling you financial advice, often quite expensive, over $10,000 in some cases, and getting you to switch into certain products".

"We still want to see greater protections and obligations on the social media platforms to ensure that these ads are taken down if there are still harmful ones being put up," he said.

Xavier O'Halloran wants to see obligations on social media platforms to take down harmful ads. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"We don't want to see claims made that can't be substantiated. We don't want to see people's details collected then on-sold to someone else without their knowledge.

"We don't want … what is meant to be a basic health check on their superannuation, then suddenly sold into very expensive financial advice that sees them switched into really inappropriate products and have their entire retirement savings wiped out."

CSLR changes could impact payouts

Today, Mr Mulino is also expected to announce changes to the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR), which covers victims of financial misconduct who have not been compensated for their losses — up to $150,000.

He is expected to widen the number of sectors that pay the levy to fund the scheme, which will include big super funds.

The "but for" test, which considers whether a claimant would have been in a better financial position had they received appropriate advice and earned interest, is expected to be removed.

The "but for" test has faced criticism from some in the advice industry for using a definition that's too broad, but consumer groups argue that removing it punishes victims of misconduct.

Stronger obligations on super platforms to check the investments they offer and act when things go wrong are also anticipated, along with stronger powers for ASIC to make platforms pay if they fail to protect their customers.

Mr Mulino is expected to unveil financial advice reforms to make financial advice more affordable and accessible to a broader range of consumers.

Michael Johnson said he and his wife Caroline had made a complaint to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) to recover their super lost in the First Guardian collapse, but that the body was still investigating their claim.

If their claim fails, or if AFCA cannot recover the money from UGC, the couple will have to rely on the CSLR.

The CSLR will treat the couple's claims as one claim, and the $150,000 cap falls well short of their total losses.

Mr Johnson said if their retirement money had stayed in performing superannuation funds, he estimated that, together, they would have accumulated about $1.3 million in retirement savings by now.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

Super Consumers' Mr O'Halloran was concerned removing the "but for" test would punish consumers and urged victims of the First Guardian and Shield collapses to claim before it is removed.

"For a typical person that was invested in Shield and First Guardian — if they don't get their complaint in by July 1 of 2027 — they could miss out on any investment earnings that they would have otherwise received in compensation," he said.

Mr O'Halloran said people who lost their life savings in the Shield and First Guardian collapses lost an average of $100,000, and Super Consumers' modelling found the government's proposed change could cost them another $26,500 in lost investment earnings.

" We don't think victims should be punished for the collapse of these financial schemes. They should be properly compensated and we [the government and regulators] should go after the actual criminals. "

Mary Delahunty, chief executive of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), welcomed the changes to ensure unlicensed lead generation operators were banned.

But she was unhappy that super funds were being tapped to pay for growing claims under the CSLR.

"It is not okay that superannuation funds have been co-opted into paying for a scheme that the majority of their members cannot claim from," Ms Delahunty said.

"What that amounts to is like a tax on every Australian to pay for a scheme that, yes, needs to exist, but not in its unsustainable form.

"So this is an ongoing point that we need to work with the government on."

Mary Delahunty says super funds should not be tapped to pay for the CSLR levy. (ABC News: Paul Pandoulis)

Sarah Abood, CEO of the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA), welcomed the minister's expected change to broaden the scope of financial advice consumers can access.

"Financial advice has never been more important, but too many Australians simply cannot afford it," she said.

"Australians need a financial advice system that is affordable, accessible and trustworthy."

Watch The Business, Mondays to Thursdays 8:44pm on ABC News Channel, after the Late News on ABC TV, and anytime on ABC iview

World.title: Cannabis use and psychosis are linked, but study finds age matters
World.content:
Cannabis-users who develop psychosis in their 30s experience symptoms more than six years earlier on average than people with the condition who don't use the drug, according to new research.

These figures are in sharp contrast to younger age groups, with cannabis-users in their early 20s who develop psychosis doing so on average about 1.6 years earlier than non-users, and no evidence of earlier onset in those under 20.

The study's senior author, University of New South Wales (UNSW) researcher Matthew Large, said the association between using cannabis and the early onset of psychosis had already been suggested by previous studies.

But in this new large-scale analysis, published today in Biological Psychiatry, Dr Large said researchers were able to examine an "enormous amount of data" and use "fine grain analysis" to look at age sub-groups for the first time.

People experiencing psychosis often feel disconnected from reality, and struggle to distinguish between what's real and what isn't.

The older the age group was, Dr Large explained, the larger gap there was between cannabis-users and non-users in regards to the age when symptoms of psychosis first appeared.

"It was widely assumed that the earlier age of onset of [psychosis] mostly affected young people. This study shows, contrary to that expectation, that it mostly affects people in their late 20s and over 30s," he said.

" That is a finding that has not been demonstrated in any other study, [it] hasn't even been suggested. "

About 2.5 million people in Australia use cannabis every year. (Getty Images: Creative Images Lab)

The study's lead author, UNSW academic and medical student Carly Stevens, said this suggested the harm could be "cumulative".

"There seems to be this predominant idea of the adolescent brain being very vulnerable, which is true," she said.

Using cannabis at a young age can disrupt neurodevelopmental processes in the adolescent brain, influencing how the brain develops, affecting the memory, attention and growth.

"But also this prevailing myth that if you wait until your brain develops, and then you engage in these kind of behaviours, that you'll be OK," she said.

"But our findings likely show that in terms of the onset of psychosis, it's not younger people that are at risk, but actually older people."

Earlier in life, Ms Stevens said genetic vulnerability and neurodevelopmental factors could play a greater role as there was very little time for cannabis to have an influence.

But, she said, ongoing cannabis use could lower the threshold for when symptoms of psychosis first appeared later in life.

More data, same results

Dr Large, who is a clinician and works directly with patients, said about 3 per cent of people will experience psychosis at some point in their lives and 1 per cent will develop schizophrenia, which is a lifelong condition.

A similar large-scale analysis led by Dr Large and published in 2011 probed 83 studies and found the mean age of psychosis onset for cannabis-users was 2.7 years younger than non-users.

This new analysis, which looked at 149 international studies involving more than 71,000 people, suggested the age of psychosis onset for cannabis-users was 2.5 years earlier, on average.

Dr Large said the similarities between the two suggested the overall conclusion was robust.

Cannabis and psychosis: how strong is the risk? Psychotic disorders are severe mental health condition and there's consistent evidence showing a link between heavy or repeated cannabis use and an experience of psychosis for the first time.

Jack Wilson, a research fellow at The University of Sydney's Matilda Centre who did not contribute to the study, said it added to "the growing body of evidence" that cannabis use was associated with a greater risk of developing psychosis.

"It's certainly providing new evidence on the likelihood of developing psychotic disorders in different age groups, according to whether someone is using cannabis or not," he said.

"And that is quite concerning, given the relative ease at which we can now access increasingly potent cannabis products in Australia."

Dr Wilson said higher consumption of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC was "associated with the greater risk of harm".

One of the study's limitations was that it didn't probe the type of cannabis products that were being used, Dr Wilson said, and extra information about potency would be useful to know.

With about 2.5 million Australians using cannabis a year, Dr Large said he was also concerned that cannabis potency was increasing over time, describing some as "amazingly potent".

Young people still at risk

Despite the study's stark findings about older Australians who use cannabis, Ms Stevens said it was important to note that younger people were certainly not immune to harm.

"Everyone, no matter the age, is at risk of some kind of adverse event from using cannabis," she said.

Dr Wilson agreed, adding that the accelerated onset of psychosis was just one measure of harm.

"There is no safe time to use cannabis, but the most dangerous or the most harmful time to use cannabis is at a younger age, particularly before the age of 25, when we're still seeing neurodevelopment," he said.

While more research was needed, Dr Wilson said changes in the developing brain could contribute to the development of psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia.

If possible, Dr Wilson urged people to avoid more potent products, which had the potential to cause not just psychosis, but greater overall harm.

"Delay the onset of use. We know that harm is greatest in those that are using cannabis at a younger age," he said.

"We also know that you know that smoking cannabis is associated with cardiovascular risk, so if people can avoid smoking and perhaps avoid mixing with tobacco."

Prompting calls for more health warnings

Researchers are now calling for greater public health messaging about the use of cannabis regardless of whether it is used recreationally or as a legal medicinal product.

They would also like to see stronger regulations regarding the sale of medicinal cannabis in Australia.

Medicinal cannabis is regulated in Australia and must be prescribed by a registered healthcare professional.

Guidelines suggest it cannot be used as a first-line treatment.

Ms Stevens said as a scientist, she wasn't able to provide an in-depth answer about best-practice legislation, but said the way medicinal cannabis was being marketed and sold in Australia was "quite inappropriate".

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

She said some providers selling medicinal cannabis claimed to operate under Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) guidelines, claiming to be "fully TGA-approved".

But most medicinal cannabis products are classed as unapproved therapeutic goods, which means they have not been assessed for safety, quality or efficacy.

Dr Large was more scathing in his assessment.

"I personally think that the medicationalisation of [cannabis] has quashed the discussions about the toxicity of cannabis," he said.

" It's that part of public policy that I think will quite likely prove to be one of the biggest public health bungles in Australian history. "

World.title: Ten killed after Russian missiles hit shops in Ukrainian village
World.content:
A Russian missile attack has killed 10 people in a village in Ukraine's north-eastern Kharkiv region, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, as he vowed that Kyiv would respond.

There was no immediate comment from Russia on the attack, which also injured at least 18 people, according to the regional governor.

"This morning, the Russians launched a brutal attack on a busy intersection in Pechenihy, Kharkiv region — a location with a post office and stores, surrounded only by residential buildings," Mr Zelenskyy said on X.

"We will definitely respond to this Russian strike," he added.

Reuters video from Pechenihy showed several covered bodies lying on the ground, burnt-out cars and damaged buildings.

Russia has intensified its air attacks on Ukraine over the summer, trying to exploit its smaller neighbour's critical shortage of interceptors capable of downing ballistic missiles.

Cafe and post office among shops hit

The United Nations said last week that civilian casualties from the war in Ukraine had risen by nearly a third month-on-month in July.

The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on X it was gathering information about the attack in Pechenihy and its impact on civilians.

Ukraine is upping strikes on Russia in a bid to pressure Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table. (Reuters: Alexander Kazakov)

Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

On Tuesday, Moscow's mayor said Ukraine had launched 620 drones at the Russian capital and surrounding areas, in one of Kyiv's biggest air assaults on the region.

Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians in their attacks.

The strike on Pechenihy village injured at least 18 people and damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, five stores and 15 cars, the governor of the surrounding region, Oleh Syniehubov, said on the Telegram messaging app.

According to preliminary information, Russia used two small Banderol cruise missiles in the attack, the office of Ukraine's Prosecutor General said.

A local official told public broadcaster Suspilne that the strikes had hit the central part of the village, where the cafe, post office and shops are located.

Drone hits near nuclear power plant

In a separate strike on Tuesday, local time, the International Atomic Energy Agency said a drone exploded at a bus stop used by staff of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, killing one and injuring several others.

The IAEA, the United Nations' nuclear power watchdog, in a statement on X also said the plant's director described the incident as "the worst event the plant has faced".

Russia currently controls the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant in southern Ukraine. (Reuters: Alina Smutko)

The agency, citing the plant's director, said the explosion at around 6am caused 16 casualties among staff and subcontractors, including one death and three serious injuries.

Russian forces seized the station, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of their February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and each side has since regularly accused the other of actions compromising nuclear safety.

UK backs Ukraine after Russian threat

Meanwhile, the UK's new prime minister is vowing the country will continue to support Ukraine "100 per cent", after Russia's embassy in the country threatened consequences over Kyiv's use of British-made drones.

British newspaper The Sunday Times earlier this week reported that two UK companies made drones used by Ukraine to hit Russia.

Following the report, the Russian embassy in the UK said in a statement that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences".

That led British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to publicly commit that the UK "stands 100 per cent behind Ukraine".

A spokesperson for the UK's defence ministry has also weighed in, saying that: "Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin's illegal invasion."

Reuters/AP

World.title: US calls Israeli strike on Syrian air base 'unnecessary escalation'
World.content:
The United States has condemned Israeli air strikes on a Syrian air base, labelling it an "unnecessary escalation" and insisting the new Syrian government is not the threat the Netanyahu government argues it is.

Syrian state television has reported eight Israeli airstrikes hit the Abu al-Duhur base in the north west of the country, 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.

The Ekhbariya outlet reported the base's runway and storage facilities were hit, citing a Syrian military source.

The Israeli military has yet to comment.

In a statement, the Syrian foreign ministry condemned the attacks and described them as an "unjustified act of aggression, a flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".

It said the "Syrian state has exercised restraint and worked to consolidate stability and avoid escalation" with Israel, despite coming under repeated attacks since early December 2024, when the former Assad regime was toppled.

That sentiment was shared by the US Ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack.

"The Al-Sharra government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces," he posted on X.

"It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel.

"The United States has in the past, and will continue in the future, to host discussions to encourage diplomatic cadence over kinetic frustration for both nations."

Mr Barrack said countries should "prioritise logical discourse over further military incidents".

Israel at odds with US over closer Syria ties

Benjamin Netanyahu's Israeli administration has expressed its deep concerns about the new Syrian government, led by former rebel leader Ahmed Al-Sharaa.

Mr Al-Sharaa, a former Al Qaeda commander, swept to power in December 2024 as his forces ended the five-decade long Assad family dictatorship.

While publicly stating he wants to unify the civil war-ravaged country, Israel has cited Mr Al-Sharaa's history and ties to extreme Islamist ideology to justify its own "security" measures against Syria.

Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa said he aims to unify the war torn country. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

This has included deploying Israeli forces into south-western Syria, beyond the border of the occupied Golan Heights, and launching strikes on some towns and cities in the area.

On Tuesday, Israel’s Foreign Ministry pointed to video which had spread on social media over the weekend purportedly showing Syrian soldiers chanting violent and threatening remarks against Jews.

Why did Israel reject Gaza plan? Israel's rejection of Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan is not a surprise. Here's why and how politics plays into it ahead of an Israeli election.

It has put Israel at odds with the United States, and particularly Donald Trump's White House, which has fostered deeper ties with the new Syrian government.

That has included lifting crippling economic sanctions against Syria, and even inviting the president to the White House — a move which would have been unthinkable just a few years ago, when Mr Al-Sharaa was subject of a US bounty.

In recent months, the Syrian government has tried to rebuild the country's air force — something Israel has seen as another threat to its own security.

With Reuters

World.title: Controversial changes to NDIS will pass after Labor strikes deal with Coalition
World.content:
The federal government will pass reforms that it says will save the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) "from itself" by making it more sustainable and cracking down further on fraud.

The Coalition voted with Labor to pass the sweeping changes in the Senate this evening, which are intended to curb the structural bloat of a scheme that costs more than $50 billion annually.

The overhaul is expected to save an estimated $37.8 billion over the next four years alone.

Health Minister Mark Butler argued the scheme had become a "soft target for shonks, for fraudsters and for sharp practice".

Mr Butler said the 63 amendments, following engagement with the disability community, reflect a "government that is willing to listen".

Powerful testimonies heard at NDIS inquiry The key takeaways from the six-day Senate inquiry into a proposed NDIS shake-up.

"We said when we announced this plan in April that we would engage deeply with the disability community but also with other parliamentarians," he told reporters this afternoon.

NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said the changes would "deliver a NDIS that is strong, safe and sustainable and has a strong social licence".

The changes include establishing an escalation pathway for high-risk participants.

Ms McAllister said it would ensure an individual requiring 24-hour continuous care could apply for a plan variation to have their needs met, protecting them from support cuts.

Jenny McAllister says the changes will deliver a more sustainable NDIS. (Matt Roberts/ABC News)

The legislation will strengthen anti-fraud measures, introducing new criminal and civil penalties for providers who offer or provide kickbacks.

It will also grant additional whistleblower protections and greater enforcement powers for the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) to ensure swifter regulatory action against unsafe or unethical providers.

The health minister said the new eligibility system, which aims to reduce participants from roughly 760,000 to 600,000 by 2030, is not explicitly spelled out in the bill.

Jordan Steele-John says the government's changes represent the end of the NDIS as it was promised. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Under the proposal, standardised assessments of functional capacity would determine eligibility for the scheme rather than diagnosis alone.

Mr Butler reassured Australians that the new eligibility standards will be made clear well ahead of their introduction on first January 2028.

The Greens have expressed concern the changes will leave hundreds of thousands without support, arguing they represent the "end of the NDIS as it was promised".

"Labor and the Liberals have got together in a room and have decided to strip us of our rights regardless of our safety or dignity," Greens senator Jordan Steele-John said this afternoon.

Crossbenchers and disability advocates also insisted the changes have come "too far, too fast".

Butler issues state warning over Thriving Kids

Mr Butler acknowledged there was still "substantial" work to do on foundational support systems for children over the age of eight and other adults who will be taken off the scheme as a result of changes.

He remained adamant that the Thriving Kids program was on track to meet its scheduled start of October 1, despite the Queensland state government's refusal to sign up to the scheme.

Asked whether he had used the $25 billion in public hospital funding to state and territories in exchange for supporting the NDIS reform as leverage, Mr Butler reminded them of their commitments.

Mark Butler says amendments made to the bill show the government is willing to listen. (Matt Roberts/ABC News)

"It's a question of honour, really, for states — they signed an agreement earlier this year that set up five years of very significant increases for our public hospital system, but a reaffirmation of the commitment they made in 2023 to work with the Commonwealth to get the NDIS back on track."

"The Queensland government needs to answer for its inability so far to live up to the agreement that the premier signed earlier this year," he added.

The ABC has approached Queensland Minister for Families, Seniors and Disability Services, Amanda Camm, for comment.

The government vowed to fast-track a fix to the unintended "widow tax" created by its changes to negative gearing in exchange for the Coalition's support.

It is part of a broader deal with the Coalition that will also create a pathway to pass Labor's gambling reforms and news media bargaining incentive.

World.title: Sydney Swans say players 'in serious breach' of club standards
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly connected to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

The ABC understands four players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are linked to an investigation into an alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in east Melbourne in the early hours of yesterday morning.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

Victoria Police is investigating, stating this morning that "the exact circumstances are yet to be established and … no one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time".

The club said it interviewed all the players linked to the incident in Melbourne and concluded "firm action" should be taken relating to the breaching of club standards.

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and Isaac Heeney are understood to be linked to a sexual assault investigation. (ABC News/Getty Images)

"The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount," a statement read.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.

"We also want to acknowledge that the care and welfare of our AFLW athletes and staff is of the utmost importance to us as a club.

"They have been and will continue to be offered the support they require, and we acknowledge the impact these allegations have on our female athletes, staff members and the wider community."

Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon did not appear at Swans HQ with the rest of their team today and were interviewed by the club off-site with lawyers present.

The Swans board will meet tonight to agree on club-imposed sanctions and penalties.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

"Any further sanctions or decisions regarding the outcome of the police investigation would take place after that process is completed," the statement read.

"During this time, we will provide the appropriate support to the players involved in the incident, along with their partners and families.

"The Sydney Swans hold all players and staff at the club to high standards of behaviour and personal conduct. Representing this club carries significant responsibilities both on and off the field, and we expect those standards to be upheld at all times.

"Our focus remains on cooperating fully with the AFL and authorities, maintaining the integrity of the process, and upholding the high standards expected of everyone who represents this club."

'Deeply concerning' incident: AFL CEO

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the allegations around the Swans were "deeply concerning", stressing that, regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, the incident raised wider concerns around the game.

"The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning," he said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon said the effects on a club's season had no bearing on the seriousness of the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport.

"The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected.

"It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course."

Dillon alluded to discussions around the potential sanctions or distractions for the Swans and the potential impact that may have on the second-placed club heading into the AFL finals.

"Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season," he said ahead of the team's final home-and-away game on Sunday.

"Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us.

"As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

"Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.

"Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light."

World.title: Mistrial declared in alleged 2007 stabbing murder at Adelaide party
World.content:
A mistrial has been declared in the case of Kimlong Rim, who is charged with murder over the alleged fatal stabbing of a 21-year-old at a birthday party almost 20 years ago.

Mr Rim, 38, had been standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to the murder of Thea Kheav outside a party at Parafield Gardens, in Adelaide's north, in December 2007.

The court previously heard Mr Kheav was a guest at the 18th birthday party, which he attended with his brothers, before he died.

Justice Rachael Gray said there would be a retrial.

World.title: Give renters a break: Two-year leases plan to protect from ‘gouging’ landlords
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Give renters a break: Two-year leases plan to protect from ‘gouging’ landlords Shane Wright August 19, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Renters would be offered at least two-year tenancy deals and billions of taxpayers’ dollars spent on new public housing under a plan from the ACTU as it pushes for the Albanese government to build on its negative gearing and capital gains tax reforms. As new figures suggest tentative signs of a slowdown in runaway rents, particularly in regional parts of the country, the union movement believes the nation’s millions of tenants need greater protection from “rent-gouging professional landlords”. The peak body for Australian unions wants to fight for two-year leases. Peter Rae The ACTU backed the May budget overhaul of property taxes that, combined with higher interest rates and low affordability, have contributed to a slowdown in property prices. Economists are tipping falls of up to 14.5 per cent in Sydney over the next 18 months before a recovery in 2028. The drop in prices comes off a peak that has left almost every capital city among the most expensive in the world. Rents have also soared by more than 20 per cent since the end of the freeze on increases introduced during the early stages of the COVID pandemic.



ACTU president Michele O’Neil said there had to be better protections for renters, especially over the length of their tenancy agreements. Loading She said the minimum tenancy should be increased from one year to two, with renters able to negotiate a shorter period if they wanted. “Our housing system should reflect the reality that millions of working people are renters. Workers deserve not only secure jobs, but also secure housing. Unions want to see renters with stronger rights, better protections against evictions and more secure leases,” O’Neil said. “Doubling the default rental standard from one to two years would still allow renters to choose shorter leases, but it would give workers more certainty and stability to plan their lives.”



On top of longer leases, unions want a national regulator of all rentals and tighter eviction procedures. Related Article Property prices Air is coming out of the housing bubble. Is now the time for first home buyers? Apart from increasing tenure security for renters, the ACTU on Wednesday will also launch a campaign for a major increase in government spending on public housing.
